In the ninth month of the fifteenth year of Shunzhi, the Emperor Shizu Zhang issued an imperial edict in a letter to the National Preceptor Yulin Tongxiu:

"I, Your Majesty, consider that establishing the fundamental principles and setting forth the regulations serves to disseminate governance and transform customs and traditions; while realizing one's nature and clarifying the mind serves to transmit the teachings."

To enlighten the people and awaken the world, one examines their achievements and finds that their undertakings follow divergent paths; yet when discussing their subtle essence, these principles converge upon the same track.
However, to trace back to the true reality of non-arising (*anutpāda*), one does not seek realization through mental images or signs;

to manifest the wondrous source of Prajñā, one does not rely on written words. If you wish to inquire about the path to enlightenment throughout the great trichiliocosm, you must first take refuge in the non-dual ferry.
Relying on the arrival of the First Patriarch, the Dharma robes have never ceased to descend.

Lighting lamps to illuminate the darkness of ignorance and striking drums to awaken the deaf and foolish, he pointed out the ferry of skillful guidance and extensively bestowed the power of expedient means.

Entrusting the Dharma for over a hundred generations, those known by name exceed a thousand; there are none who do not together uphold the fundamental tenets and greatly propagate the enduring tradition.
With compassion, you deliver all under heaven, assisting in the establishment of peace and governance to transform the lives of the people;

thus, you have truly contributed to this flourishing era and have been held in constant honor throughout successive generations. Now we hear that you, the monk Tongxiu, possess wisdom that penetrates the beginningless and an insight that fathoms True Suchness (*tathatā*).

You continue the orthodox lineage of the Five Patriarchs, through whom the myriad dharmas are brought back to their unity; you have cleared away the perverse consciousnesses of the six sense-faculties, and [realized that] the four great elements are...
Having swept away the wild Chan of the degenerate age with the broom of ultimate emptiness and upheld the True Enlightenment of the Tathāgata,

he truly transcends the learning of Zhaosheng and Daorong and has widely disseminated his reputation for contemplation and emulation. As I humbly consult those who possess the Dharma-vessel and reminisce about his lofty style,

I have long hoped since ascending the throne to pour forth the governance of non-action (*wuwei*), and I sit here in vacancy awaiting him, joyfully wishing to hear his teachings on the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).

For this reason, I have specially dispatched Zhang Jiamu, the official in charge of the seals at the Bureau of Officials, to bestow upon you this imperial edict and extend a distant invitation for you to take up your staff and alms bowl.

May you hasten your journey on your elephant-like carriage and arrive early at the Dragon Steps. There, you shall set forth the wisdom of the emptiness of profound principles and assist in the purity of our imperial governance.
Alas! If one asks about me while following the wind, I shall surely go together with you to seek the Way at Mount Kongtong; let us count the days until we meet.
Since that time, you have continued to emulate the rivers of the Han and Jiang that flow toward the capital; be reverent! Thus I instruct you.

Furthermore, in the fourth month of the sixteenth year of the Shunzhi era, I reflected upon how the teachings were propagated in Western India and the Dharma spread to this eastern land, entrusting the wondrous mind to the four and seven patriarchs and transmitting the true fruit to... [the successors].

Among the two or three [patriarchs], there were none who did not achieve thorough penetration through realization; those whose practice was pure and unified were considered true vessels of the Dharma.
Thus, Nanyue did not defile [the lineage] and extended his protective mindfulness at Yuling; Mazu’s Great Function resounded with the "Ho! shout atop Xiongfeng.
Furthermore, Huangbo established his school by the Huoshui River, and Gao Feng continued the succession of Xueyan; the source is thus profound and far-reaching.

That this tradition has such a long and noble lineage is for good reason. I have exhausted my heart in sincerity and rectitude, humbled my will amidst the subtle and the minute, striving to reach the shore of the Way and aspiring to ascend grandly to the realm of true virtue.

Yet, in the cultivation of virtue, there is often no conscious awareness. This leads me to reflect that the pacification of the self and the establishment of government must both be rooted in the realization of nature and the clarification of the mind.
The Great Way is fundamentally one; its refined principles are non-dual. Looking back upon our ancestral lineages, there must surely be eminent sages—have you heard of them?
The Chan Master Tongxiu is a direct successor of Linji and a close descendant of Xiyuan; his mind-source is pure and his practice and realization are solitary and lofty.
Therefore, in the autumn of the Wuxu year, I specially dispatched an imperial envoy to invite him to the capital.

He took up residence at Shangling Park, and during my leisure from state affairs, I personally inquired into the profundities of the Buddhist teachings. Observing that his spiritual acumen was sharp and incisive, I [found him] to be... [discourse].
His realization is perfectly complete as he directly points toward the ultimate threshold; his faith is truly accurate as he penetrates the principle of non-arising.

Not falling into the trap of verbal explanations, he has truly attained my own heart and deeply accords with my own aspirations. Occasionally he ranges over various doctrines and broadly synthesizes the teachings of the hundred schools;
his reasoning constantly transcends the mundane, resolving doubts without obstruction. He is truly a dragon or elephant among the Dharma gates and a lion among the Zen gardens.
He was a true Jewel of the Forest. For this reason, an imperial decree was specially bestowed to grant him the title "Great Awakened One" (Dajue).

Just as he was about to remain long with his alms-bowl and robes while listening to the sounds of the *gāthā*, I hoped that by attending upon him morning and evening, we might together silently fulfill the ultimate purpose.

However, the Chan Master wished to complete his filial duty and exhaust his thoughts of devotion, firmly requesting to return to the mountains to diligently assist in the construction of a stone stupa, thereby following in the distant footsteps of Maudgalyāyana.

As for this Lady Duomu, who recently received the support of the venerable elder Chen to care for her parents—thereby benefiting human relations and rectifying social customs—I have humbly acceded to her wish and issued an imperial decree to escort her back swiftly.
Alas, the mountains and rivers are so distant that summer and autumn have already passed between us;
yet as I reflect upon her enduring legacy, she remains earnestly in my heart. Recalling the words she spoke in our presence, they truly reveal the secrets of the Mahāyāna.
That the transmission of the lamp may continue is what is most hoped for in these final dharma-ages;
thus, I have again bestowed a gracious edict to confer the title of Chan Master Dajue Pujie, granted him purple robes and a golden seal, and dispatched an envoy to deliver them.

This manifests my profound regard and serves to further illuminate the seat of the Dharma, forever securing it as a treasure of the mountain gate. Alas! With the imperial dragon-script now conferred, the Sun of Wisdom is further augmented.

Having been newly bestowed with radiant and magnificent robes, you are able to succeed to the Dharma-robe of the Buddha; we pray that you may uphold this manifest mandate and further exert yourself in diligent cultivation.
Be reverent! Thus we decree.
Furthermore:
Since I first took up my staff and returned south, I have constantly yearned for the misty scenery of the Five Lakes and the elegant beauty of the Three Rivers;

clad in lotus robes and feeding on pine needles, there is truly enough to bring joy. When the wind from the Changhe Gate arrives, the autumn colors linger with lingering grace, and the white dew deepens my longing for that person.
From this recent time onward, I have sought out the Chan school and applied myself diligently to the Dharma-treasure, lamenting that since the time of Foguo and Ying’an, [the lineage has declined].
The world has recently grown quiet; though the thunderous voice of the Dharma now resounds, it is as if it has not yet been heard in the north.

Consequently, among the bhikṣus of this final dharma age, few honor the precepts and Vinaya. Those who speak of non-existence while their conduct remains within existence are as rare as hemp or millet seeds.
It is therefore my desire to establish a Royal Altar in the capital, so that a community of fifteen hundred monastics may receive the *vinaya*.
The seven precepts and a single thread originate from the Upper Realm; the five precepts and the three refuges are a solemn proclamation of the Buddha’s teachings.

Yet, this is not because the Chan Master personally performed the *karmavācanā* (ordination ritual); it is truly out of concern that the supreme vessel of compassion serves as a ladder for humans and devas.

I only hope that you will take up the burden of the Tathāgata and elucidate the Great Dharma, not declining the long journey and graciously consenting to come; then, within the four gates of the imperial city—
Having repeatedly heard the fragrance of the campaka flowers, the newly ordained monks have suddenly seen the tree of Bodhi grow;
they know that the Chan Master prioritizes the great matter of the Buddha-dharma rather than being preoccupied with minor matters of quiet seclusion and withdrawal.
Gazing afar toward Fudu, they are swiftly comforted in their long-held longing.
In the twelfth month of the fortieth year of the Kangxi era, the Emperor Shengzu Renhuang composed the "Epigraph for the Putuo Shan Pujisi Temple.
Examining the Sanskrit texts, it is found that there are three Mount Potalakas: one is located in Uṇṇata-kṣetra, and one is located in... [text fragment].
"Baiti" (White Teeth) is located in the South Sea; it is a mountain. The original records of this mountain have not been obtained in full detail.
In those days, when pirates were rampant, all temples and monasteries beyond the forbidden seas were reduced to ashes.
Since the pacification of Taiwan in the twenty-second year of the Kangxi era, the waves have forever subsided; thus, wandering monks [reconstructed] [the site] based on the old foundations.
Having cleared away the brambles, thistles, and weeds to restore it to its former splendor, I, the Emperor, while on a tour of inspection in Western Zhejiang,

specially dispatched an official to reverently prepare pure offerings and respectfully inscribed the plaque for the mountain gate to ensure its eternal stability. Furthermore, I issued treasury funds to rebuild the temple buildings,

ensuring that the halls, corridors, and windows were resplendent with vermilion and green hues, and that the rafters and beams were magnificently adorned, so that every piece of wood and every stone was [perfectly restored].
By assigning one man to one service from the public treasury, the people’s labor is not burdened;

above, it extends longevity to my compassionate mother, and below, it bestows blessings upon all living beings. Since my youth, I have studied the classics and histories, taking the principles of self-cultivation, family regulation, state governance, and world peace as my foundation;
I have had no leisure to peruse the golden sutras and palm-leaf manuscripts concerning emptiness, stillness, or the nature of foam and shadows.
Being unable to fathom its inner sanctum, I shall speak of it in general terms: "The Origin (*yuan*) is the foremost of all that is good. The Buddha takes goodness as his foundation;

when this principle is extended and expanded, it is roughly no different [from our own teaching]. The Supreme Heaven’s love for transformation and its nurturing of the myriad species, and the Great Being’s compassion in delivering all sentient beings—these two are likewise no different.
For over forty years, I have sought to govern and diligently labored for the people.

Now that arms and armor have been laid aside, yet the livelihoods of the people have not yet reached a state of peace and abundance; though the stubborn and wayward have been transformed, the hearts of the people are not yet entirely pure and good.
This is because floods and droughts are irregular and harvests vary between plenty and scarcity—a matter with which I am tirelessly preoccupied, day and night, unable to set it from my mind.
By the power of the Great Being (Mahāsattva), may there arise the compassionate clouds, the Dharma-rain, the nectar-like dew, and the auspicious winds.

If the years are bountiful and the people are at peace, and if the myriad subjects enjoy benevolence and longevity, then this will constitute the grand merit of universal salvation and the supreme order of the realm;
this is my heart’s desire. Thus, these words are inscribed upon wooden tablets and engraved upon a lofty monument to be transmitted for eternity.
Furthermore, the Imperially Composed Stele Inscription for the Reconstruction of Tianzhu Temple states:

"I, the Emperor, presiding over the profound tranquility of the universe, have extended my concern throughout the four quarters. In surveying the lands and establishing the teachings, my imperial carriage halted at this mountain and lake; I look with affection upon these people."
As for the power [of this place] in the southeast, how could it merely be known as a scenic wonder of the Imperial Chariot?

Rather, by following its ancient traces and avoiding ostentation toward former spectacles, this is the reason why the Tianzhu Monastery was renovated. Indeed, while Vulture Peak is renowned in the West, the Dharma Wheel is singular;
and while the Zhu Peak is magnificent in the Southern Land, these three famous monasteries remain the very places where the clergy and laity cultivate their practice.
It is also the cave-dwelling of immortals and spirits; the sound of the tide echoes afar, connecting with Putuo, while the shadow of the pagoda spans the void, long preserving the śarīra relics.
Auspicious light radiates above the mountain stream, and wondrous trees manifest the countenance of the Great Being (Bodhisattva).

Moved by a dream, the White-Robed One established a temple for reciting scriptures within this pure realm; when droughts occurred and the grain and wheat were on the verge of withering, banners and canopies [were raised].
When heavy rains come, they drench one's feet; yet when prayers are offered, they are immediately answered, and blessings arrive without fail.

This has indeed been the case from the Jin and Song dynasties down to the present, and it is recorded in the annals as something worthy of belief. It seems that the capacity of the Benevolent One (Śākyamuni) is equal to his love for all living beings, and the perfection of the Buddha-way is intimately connected to the hidden sufferings of the people.
Considering this principle, is it not truly magnificent? It shall cause the Prajñā...

The gates [to enlightenment] open according to the direction, and the realm of benevolent longevity allows the entire world to ascend together; since such a flourishing state exists, how could it be abandoned?
In the past, I personally attended my compassionate mother at her residence and visited these halls.
Looking westward from Lake Fang and proceeding southward along the carriage path toward the First Stage (Prathama-bhūmi), I passed by this site.

Flowers welcome the returning banners as clouds unroll over the deep crags; the milk-caves hold the precious luster of true pearls, and the peaks turn like those that flew hither, bearing the azure hue of lapis lazuli.
Protected by a hundred spirits, the Seven Sages do not lose their way.
Having offered prayers for the longevity and well-being of our Empress Dowager, we further hope that all these common people shall enjoy abundant joy within their households. Thus, Ka...
How could the vast compassion of Śākyamuni differ from the virtue bestowed by our state?

Reflecting upon the mountain spirits as they were of old, yet observing that the appearance of the temple has not been renewed, our Imperial Grandmother has given rise to the aspiration for the sake of the nation and offered prayers for the blessing of the people; thus she has repeatedly [issued this decree].
By Your compassionate decree, the Xianglin Monastery has been reconstructed; the undertaking of this project shall not interfere with the affairs of the people.

As it rises to the clouds once more in splendor, will there not be the spiritual resonance of the Land of the Buddha? May it be accomplished in no time, truly solidifying the blessings of the Great Earth.
May the lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges ascend together with the Realm of Eternal Bliss, and may the hundreds of millions of sentient beings enjoy boundless peace. This, then, is my—
The Sage Heart of the Empress Dowager remains that of a Kāśyapa,
and it is precisely this that accords with my own mind in governing the world and bringing benefit and salvation to all living beings.
On the eighteenth day of the sixth month of the first year of the Yongzheng era,
the Emperor Shizong Xianhuangdi issued a vermilion edict in response to the memorial submitted by Li Fu, Governor-General of Zhejiang,
further instructing him: "Tracing the transmission of the Way from Yao and Shun down to the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, the sages have succeeded one another."

To concentrate on the One without distraction is fundamentally independent of the teachings of Śākyamuni or Laozi. Since the Han dynasty, the three teachings have been transmitted like the brilliance of the Three Luminaries, standing firm like the three legs of a tripod;
that they have not been abandoned or fallen into ruin for over a thousand years—is this not because their paths proceed side by side without contradicting one another?
Our Confucians rectify the mind and cultivate nature; the followers of Śākyamuni clarify the mind and realize nature; and the practitioners of the Original Gate (Taoism) cultivate...

If we speak of the substance (*tǐ*)—refining the mind to cultivate the nature—it is identical to the Sage’s “enlightening the self and transforming the people,” the Tathāgata’s “benefiting oneself and benefiting others,” and the Supreme Lord’s “immeasurable deliverance of beings. If we speak of its function (*yòng*), it is likewise identical:
as the *Zhōngyōng* says, “be cautious regarding what is unseen and fearful regarding what is unheard”; and as the Inner Canon says, “the six sense-objects encounter their respective realms.”
The mind does not follow external conditions; as the *Daodejing* says, "Not seeing that which excites desire keeps the mind from being disturbed.

In terms of the practice of spiritual cultivation, this is likewise no different. Yet, why is it that inferior scholars often employ narrow, biased views to engage in contentious debate and indulge their own preconceptions?
This is because they judge solely on the basis of outward appearances and fail to penetrate its profound depths.
Regarding the statement that the teachings of these two schools (Buddhism and Daoism) have no connection whatsoever to the way of the world or the hearts of the people—

who would know that this is not so? For the principle that "a family that accumulates goodness will surely have an abundance of blessings, while a family that accumulates evil will surely have an abundance of calamity" is recorded in the *Book of Changes* (*Zhouyi*),
and the meaning that the retribution for good and evil follows like a shadow following a form is clearly set forth in the *Gan* (The Response).
The secret principles regarding the causal cycle of rebirth within the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence are scattered throughout the various sutras of the Great Canon.

Whether it be through warnings and reminders, or through guidance and encouragement, these teachings fit together like the two halves of a tally; when their ultimate aim is examined, they are nothing other than exhorting people to do good.
This applies whether one considers the humble settings of inner chambers and village lanes, or the distant reaches of coastal shores and mountain fastnesses.
There are those who cannot be sustained by rites and music, nor guided by the Odes and the Books;

yet the teachings of these two [Buddhist and Daoist] schools are both sufficient to inspire sincere devotion and to eliminate their hidden and subtle vices. Viewed from this perspective, how could Buddhism and Daoism possibly fail to provide benefit to the royal transformation of the people?
Let us ask: of these three paths, would the Middle Kingdom choose to eliminate two and retain one?
Is one person capable [of this], or not? If not, why must they divide into schools and establish separate houses, mutually excluding one another as if in a mass of litigation?
Behold this age of the Dharma’s decline: among those wearing the yellow caps and black robes, the ignorant and foolish predominate;

for the most part, they are merely hungry men and lazy fellows who seek only gain and sustenance. Consequently, monasteries and hermitages have ultimately become places that harbor filth and tolerate impurity.
This is like having weeds among grain or chaff among millet; it lies solely in distinguishing which is the grain and which is the weed.
How could one possibly discard both the grain and the millet together? I have long held the Three Teachings in equal esteem and venerated them as one body;

in my observance of the rites for honoring the Buddhas and respecting the Immortals, I have never been the least bit negligent. Yet, whenever I see those scholars of the Confucian classics who hold the other two in contempt...
This gentleman was habitually prone to contempt and exclusion, being especially severe toward those who claimed the name of "Principle-Student" (Lixue).

Upon examining his actual conduct and its comparison with the true essence of Principle-Student learning, they were found to be utterly at variance; he was nothing more than one of those like the frog in the well or the quail in the fence.
How could he be worth comparing with? Zhejiang is popularly known as the "Sea of Monks," a place where monks have long established their lodgings; it has been so for nearly ten years.
The arrival of such individuals is not limited to those like Yueqing, whose spiritual resonance and monastic style are rarely seen;
even among those who are thoroughly versed in the teachings and the Vinaya, such a person has not been heard of. The decline of the monastic communities is truly lamentable.

You should embody my intention, and in the intervals of your official duties, take care to protect and sustain them so that they do not fall into excessive desolation or ruin, yet without becoming attached to outward forms.
This is for the purpose of adornment; you should understand this admonition for yourself and not let the multitude know it.
Why? Because if scholars hear of it, they will merely mock me as a "Buddhist enthusiast," and if monastics hear of it, it will cause their pride to increase.

Among those of mediocre character, some may even go so far as to abandon the foundations [of discipline] or, at worst, disrupt the pure regulations, thereby violating the laws of the Dharma in a thousand ways. It is out of pity for them that I have acted contrary [to my usual restraint].
To harm it is to conceal it.
Furthermore, on the nineteenth day of the fourth month in the second year of the Yongzheng era,
an Imperial Edict was issued to the Grand Secretariat concerning a previous memorial which reported that women were entering temples to offer incense in large, disorderly crowds.

Regarding those who wander about in vain waste, engage in useless activities, or enter other schools to spread delusive speech and mislead the masses—actions which ought to be prohibited—an imperial edict was previously issued permitting them to proceed;
however, this was not a prohibition against commoners prostrating themselves in famous mountains and temples.
Now we hear that all temples and monasteries are being generally prohibited, and that commoners are no longer permitted to perform kowtows or visit [the sites]. This is improper.
Those who offer incense at Mount Ji (Ji Shan) have been registering and paying taxes at the Jinzhanhé (Golden Chalice River) location, which is inconsistent with My imperial decree.
Regarding the excessive prohibitions therein, the Ministry of Rites shall investigate and submit a report to the Imperial Court;
as for the Jinzhanhé location, it is to be handed over to the Provincial Governor of Zhili, who shall investigate and submit a report.

Furthermore, on the third day of the second month in the eighth year of the Yongzheng era, an imperial vermilion edict was issued in response to the memorial submitted by Liu Shiming, Governor-General of Fujian, which stated:
"One should only prohibit heterodox sects that delude the masses; there has never been any principle for prohibiting people from observing the vegetarian fast. This memorial is most... [excellent].
This belongs to the ultimate fallacy of following a misguided vehicle; I do not understand what kind of views you hold that you speak thus.
If one were to take such irrational and reckless assertions as being the fulfillment of one's duty and the diligent execution of one's responsibilities, it would be a great error.

Since you have stated that you wish to observe the fast due to old age, let it be so; however, to further seek to cast blame upon all members of the household, both great and small, who also observe the fast, is even more improper.

This is truly laughable talk: to scrutinize whether a particular member of a household has fasted or not during the mealtime of the elderly and the young—what kind of commotion would such a thing cause?
Observe all the reports submitted for review;
they are not only superficial and unsubstantial, but often perverse and off the mark, revealing a state of great mental confusion and agitation. Hereafter...
If you still fail to earnestly admonish yourselves and exert yourselves with sincerity and reverence, my imperial favor will be truly regrettable.
Furthermore, on the fifteenth day of the second month in the eleventh year of the Yongzheng era, an Imperial Edict was issued to the Grand Council:
"I reflect that the Three Teachings enlighten the people within the realm; their principles are identical in originating from a single source."

The Original Way and the Buddha-way proceed side by side without contradiction; it is only because people cannot achieve a sudden, comprehensive realization that they each hold different minds and harbor different views.
Those who admire the Way claim that the Buddha is not as venerable as the Way; those who incline toward the Buddha claim that the Way is not as great as the Buddha;
and the Confucians, moreover, simultaneously reject both schools as heterodox, harboring private biases.
The minds of men contend for victory and refuse to yield to one another; I, however, maintain that the discourse of the Three Teachings seeks only to attain their equilibrium.
Once equilibrium is attained, one disregards external differences in form and trace while internally verifying the identity of fundamental nature and principle;
thus, one knows that the Three Teachings originally possess no divergent tenets, as they all desire that people return together to goodness. As for the Buddha...

The Five Precepts and the Ten Wholesome Actions of Buddhism guide people toward goodness; the Five Constant Virtues and the hundredfold conduct of our Confucianism likewise provide encouragement, assistance, and exhortation—how could there be even one among them that does not lead people toward doing good?
Formerly, Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty asked the Palace Attendant He Shangzhi:
"The Six Classics are fundamentally for governing the mundane world; as for the essential truths of the spiritual nature, one must take the Buddhist scriptures as one's guide."
"If the people of the entire realm all become pure through this transformation, I shall achieve Great Peace while sitting still.
He Shangzhi replied, "If ten people in a village of a hundred households observe the five precepts, those ten will become pure and conscientious.

If a hundred people in a town of a thousand houses observe the ten wholesome deeds, those hundred will be harmonious. If this moral instruction is spread throughout the world, then the registered households [will reach] a billion."
If a thousand benevolent men and a hundred thousand people can each practice one act of goodness, then one evil will be eliminated; if one evil is eliminated, then one punishment will cease.

I have carefully examined this sūtra, which exists in five translations from the Han, Wei, Wu, Tang, and Song dynasties.

Among these, the Wei translation is particularly detailed and comprehensive in its phrasing, and its principles and meanings are perfectly complete; consequently, commentators of the past have mostly relied upon it. The Tang translation is somewhat similar to it.

It appears that these were originally the same Sanskrit manuscript; yet the Song translation is also remarkably clear and fluent, while the phrasing and wording differ greatly from the preceding versions—suggesting they were derived from another Sanskrit manuscript.

Furthermore, the translations by the Han and Wu dynasties are stylistically clumsy and harsh, yet their meanings complement and complete one another, indicating they were based on yet another Sanskrit manuscript.
Having briefly examined various scriptures, I have summarized the reasons for these differences as follows:
There are three factors. First, the skill or lack thereof in the hands of the translators differs.

This is evident, for example, in the three translations of the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the six translations of the *Vajracchedikā*, and these two translations of the present short text; in such cases, while the phrasing differs slightly, the meaning remains largely the same.
This clearly demonstrates that the Sanskrit original exists in various versions. For example, when Confucian scholars interpret the classics, each has their own strengths and weaknesses.

Although he bases his explanation on the intersection of Yin and Yang energies, his insight is subtle; what seems extraordinary is actually correct. In the future, there will surely be those who understand this. Thus, those who attain rebirth...
One attains the path of transcendence, long life, and *nirvāṇa*. This is "next" (*ci*) to the path of unconditioned *nirvāṇa*. (This is the text of the Great Version of the Sūtra.

"Next" here does not mean sequential order; it refers to comparison or categorization. Since *nirvāṇa* is a name for the Tathāgata’s extinction, and one has not yet actually attained extinction, it is called "next. The *Huìshù* cites the following passage, "next like Maitreya," as evidence, which captures the true intent of the sūtra very well.
*Nirvāṇa* is the same as *niepán*. It is also called *panripan* (or *panyuepan*, where the latter is likely an error for the character for "sun"). [It is] Sanskrit.

The sounds are light and heavy accordingly. Holding up a flower to the assembly, [the Buddha] said: "I have the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye" (this refers to the wondrous clarity of the nature-awakening;

the following phrase refers to the clarity-wonder of fundamental awakening. Taken together, they constitute the Tathāgatagarbha). Generally, teachings arise from existence and are realized through cognition. However, this is knowledge that is inherently possessed, not knowledge arising from subsequent consciousness or views. Yongjia’s verse says: "One does not know stillness by means of knowing, nor does one know knowing by oneself.

It cannot be said that there is no knowing, for the self-nature is luminously clear. This is not the same as indeterminate ignorance (*avyākṛta*). Now, I take this very luminous clarity before our eyes as the True Dharma Eye, which gives rise to the separate transmission. It does not mean that there is something else. *Nirvāṇa*.

The Wondrous Mind of Perfect Enlightenment (*Banyaoxin*). (This directly points to the fact that the human mind is originally thus. It is what is called "originally unborn," and now likewise not extinguished. It is what is called "when birth and extinction have ceased, quiescent extinction manifests. To attempt to understand this through the non-arising of a single thought is a great error.

The True Mark is Without Mark (*Shixiang wuxiang*). (This is what is called "not grasping at marks; suchness is unmoving. It is what is called "knowing and seeing without seeing; this is itself *nirvāṇa*. To attempt to understand this by saying that when the mind is pure through faith in the Golden Sutra, the true mark is produced, or by reciting the name of the Buddha of the True Mark, is also a great error.

Regarding the "Subtle and Wondrous Dharma Gate" and so forth... Thus, these two— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the philosophical content of the preceding sections regarding the nature of mind and reality as presented in Zen/Chan discourse.)

What the various schools have realized is identical to this mind of nirvana; what difference could there be? Furthermore, "directly pointing to the human mind to see one's nature and become a Buddha" does not mean that one becomes a Buddha upon the very first sight [of it].

It means that once one sees one's nature, one will no longer fall into erroneous practice—such as the ten types of immortal practices described in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which instead lead to the state of external paths. Therefore, it is said: "In principle, there is sudden awakening; through awakening, all is simultaneously extinguished. In matters, there must be gradual elimination; through successive stages, they are exhausted.

Those from the middle grade of the superior birth in the Pure Land downward must all continue their cultivation until they reach the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) and the position of the successor (*abhiṣeka*). Only then is there "no cultivation and no realization," which follows the same principle. However, because there are no defiled conditions, one is able to [attain] unity.

"Birth, grasping, and completion—when one observes those in the Chan school who emerge from and submerge into this [state], the difference between ease and difficulty, or level and perilousness, is as distinct as heaven and abyss.
This is exactly the same as directly relying on the present single thought to see the Buddha and awaken to the nature; what difference could there be? (4)

Question: Since the cultivation and realization of Chan and Pure Land are identical, why do many in the Chan school claim that Pure Land is not ultimate, while this view also occasionally appears among those of the Teaching school?
Answer: These views all stem from a lack of clarity regarding the principles of the teachings; they are merely the private opinions of specific schools.

When our Original Teacher beheld the appearance of the morning star, he attained sudden and great enlightenment, whereupon he exclaimed, "How marvelous! All sentient beings possess... [the Tathāgata-garbha].
The wisdom, virtue, and marks of the Tathāgata cannot be realized because of deluded thoughts and attachments; thus, he preached the *Avataṃsaka* to lead and entice [beings].

(In the fifty-third assembly, it is said that right view is to realize that the present moment is suchness itself, and that all dharmas are nothing other than Buddha-dharma. Yet, failing to understand this, they go so far as to carve up empty space and arbitrarily divide it into boundaries.

Since most capacities did not accord with this, he instead spoke of the biased and small provisional teachings (*upāya-śāsana*) to gradually lead toward the perfect, great, and real teaching. (He divided the teachings into five periods. Having finished speaking...)

As seen previously, during the period of the Vaipulya (fangdeng) teachings, the Mahāyāna sūtras were necessarily expounded first, followed by various indications pointing toward their ultimate destination; thus, the matters and principles may be understood. Upon reaching the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the provisional was opened and the real was revealed.
In particular, the Buddha manifested the rebirth of a woman as proof and universally conferred upon the present assembly the attainment of Buddhahood, thereby fully expressing his original intent.

Thus, the fundamental tenets of the temporal teachings throughout the entire dispensation may be known. The "Holding up of the Flower" occurred after the *Lotus Sūtra*; it was prompted by Kāśyapa’s slight...

I smile. This is precisely in accord with the original vow and the conditions for awakening at the very beginning. (How could all the bodhisattvas and disciples present have failed to realize the principle that this very moment is itself suchness?)

However, for those who have long been enlightened, this has become their habitual practice; for those newly awakened, they have not yet forgotten the need for conscious maintenance. Thus, the occasional picking up of a flower is also a common occurrence. Kāśyapa’s smile is what is meant by "each time it is raised, it is renewed anew"—it was not that he only attained awakening at this moment.

Only Ānanda had not yet realized the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*); when the time came for the compilation of the scriptures, Kāśyapa urged him to do so. Therefore, at that time, he concurrently entrusted Ānanda as his deputy to propagate the teachings. Judging from the texts and inferring the underlying principles, the facts are clear. Consequently, he bestowed the entrustment upon him.
As for the claims that "no words are established" or that there is "a separate transmission outside the teachings," these refer precisely to what has been explained thus far within the teachings.
It is exhausted; there is nothing further to be said. One need only realize it for oneself; it is difficult to transmit through words. This does not mean that there is some separate dharma.
Consider the final transmission of the Dharma by the First Patriarch, Bodhidharma: he produced the four-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* to seal the mind.
This was precisely after the Lotus School had flourished and the teachings and contemplations of the Tiantai school had become greatly clarified. Then came the Second Patriarch, Shen Guang.
He had thoroughly mastered the various scriptures and was well-versed in Confucian texts;

yet the method he sought was nothing more than the single phrase, "I have finished instructing you on how to settle the mind," and the method he attained was nothing more than prostrating and standing in his place without uttering a single word.

Is this not proof that cultivation and realization remain within the teachings? (Later generations used the fact that the Sixth Patriarch was illiterate as a pretext to become mired in dogmatic adherence to the principle of "not relying on words," claiming that the essence does not lie therein. Little do they realize that...)

If one’s fundamental principle does not penetrate the teachings, one will fall into confusion as soon as the mouth opens. This is clearly evidenced by the *Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch*, which asks: "If people of the East commit offenses and seek rebirth in the West, when people of the West commit offenses, where do they seek rebirth?

This is a manifest proof of such confusion. Now, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land is certainly not for the sake of having committed offenses; the sutras explicitly state that in the Western Land, even the name of the evil realms does not exist, let alone their actual presence. How, then, could there be offenses there? These few words [of the *Platform Sutra*] greatly obstruct the principles of the teachings.

All other parts are merely practical deliberations and direct pointers to the present reality, containing nothing extraordinary; they truly represent the realm of thorough awakening. If one were to claim that all teachings regarding the Pure Land are provisional (*upāya*), then that would mean [the Pure Land teachings are inferior to] the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Regarding the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*): it is like using a willow leaf to stop a child’s crying; one’s original intent has not yet been fully realized.

Furthermore, throughout the forty-nine years [of his teaching], the four kinds of *siddhānta* have never reached the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Yet, in this single instance, is there not the principle that only Kāśyapa alone obtained the true gold?

In the tradition of the Holy Teachings, those who slander the Pure Land school are most numerous among the Xianshou (Huayan) sect, while the Tiantai sect... [is based on]... because of... (Note: The source text appears to be a fragmentary commentary on Buddhist doctrine, specifically addressing the relationship between provisional teachings and the ultimate truth, the realization of Kāśyapa, and sectarian critiques regarding the Pure Land.)

The Patriarch Zhiyi has the *Ten Doubts Treatise* (this is certainly not in the Patriarch’s own hand; how could such literary style have existed during the Chen and Sui periods? This can be known by examining his other writings.

It was likely composed by a follower of the Tiantai school in the early Tang dynasty recording his master’s teachings; thus, its reasoning is extremely precise and appropriate). Therefore, I do not dare to slander it. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is the king among all the sūtras.
The Confucians also delight in recitation and study. For instance, when Cao Luchuan debated with Master Lianchi, their exchange spanned over two thousand words;
yet it was merely empty counting of another’s treasures. They failed to realize that what the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* upholds is actually found within the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.

(From Master Ouyi’s *Essential Commentary*) Furthermore, among the eighty fascicles of the *Avataṃsaka*, the only teaching spoken by our Original Teacher is the "Asaṃkhyeya Chapter" concerning the Tathāgata’s lifespan.

The Chapter on Measure (*Pramāṇa-varga*). (In this chapter of the present sutra, it is spoken by the Bodhisattva Cittarāja; it is separately titled the *Sūtra Revealing the Merits of Boundless Buddha-lands*. In the translation by Master Xuanzang, however, it is spoken by the Teacher himself in response to the questions of King Acintyaprabhāsa.

The three chapters beginning with the "Chapter on the Merits of the Tathāgata’s Minor Marks and Radiance" (*Anuvyañjana-prabhā-guṇa-varga*) are precisely the original revelation of the Pure Land teachings of Amitābha and Amitāyus.
(Master Tiantai [Lian-shi] did not take this into account when answering Cao Luchuan; what a pity to have missed it!)

If one were to claim that the Pure Land is merely provisional, would it not follow that the bodhisattvas of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, who have already ascended to the Precious Abode, would instead be led by Samantabhadra’s Ten Great Vows back toward the illusory city on the way? Is such a principle even possible?

Generally speaking, these stubborn disputes arising from divergent approaches and views indicate that the study and practice of the teachings and contemplations have not yet been abandoned; yet, in recent decades, only the Pure Land school has remained.
The Earth School (Tudimen) adheres to the doctrine of self-power and the single mind, challenging themselves and others with such vehemence that they brandish weapons within the same room.
Unless this school is decisively severed, the situation will become increasingly alarming; therefore, I cannot help but discuss it at length.

Nevertheless, I especially hope that my fellow practitioners and eminent worthies, upon seeing their divergent tendencies, will not hastily engage them in debate. (Even the virtuous cannot avoid the desire for victory or the defense of their own positions; as for those who practice the Way, this may take several years...)

Having labored for several decades, one has likely come to feel self-satisfied; yet, to desire that one suddenly abandon oneself to follow another requires nothing short of great wisdom and great courage—something a Bodhisattva appearing in this world alone could accomplish. If one were truly able to do so, it would be like turning a single pivot, rendering further words unnecessary.

One should instead turn inward to reflect and give rise to a sense of shame and remorse. For while the other may ultimately fail to attain a state of single-mindedness, they at least do not lose their state of scattered mind (*vikṣipta-citta*).
If my own faith and aspiration are not genuine, I shall lose even that scattered mind. (This is the intended meaning of Master Lianchi’s *Shuchao*.)

Perhaps they have already perceived this, yet they did not anticipate that after a long time, corruption would arise and turn into an obstacle as it does today. If such individuals do not give rise to the mind of aspiration, then one should cite the *Sūtra of the Small Root* and the teachings of Master Ou-yi (Ouyi Zhixu) to gently exhort them.
By thus dissolving differences of opinion and joining together to support the turning wheel of the Dharma’s fortune, there may yet be hope for its revival. (5)

Question: Since ancient times, those who have spoken of mindfulness of the Buddha (nienfo) have distinguished between mindfulness of one’s own Buddha, mindfulness of another Buddha, and mindfulness of both one’s own and another Buddha.
Why is it that you now speak exclusively of mindfulness of another Buddha? Answer:

In the teachings, what is called mindfulness of the Buddha consists solely of the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha (as described in the Bhadrapāla-sūtra, cited above) and the practice of upholding the name in the Pure Land; both of these concern another Buddha. As for the Chan school...

There are those who highly extol the sacred realm while disparaging their own spiritual capacity; in response to this, there arose the teaching of "reciting the name of one's own Buddha" (such as the inquiry, "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?").
To harmonize these views through the perfect integration characteristic of the Pure Land school, there arose the teaching of "reciting the names of both one's own Buddha and the Buddhas of others.

In reality, the subtle excellence of the Pure Land Dharma gate lies in the exclusive recitation of the Buddhas of others. This is evident in the *Lengyan wenju* (Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra) and the *Zhiji*... [text truncated]

This refers to the chapter on the Great Power Attainment (Mahāsthāmaprāpta) as the most definitive among the chapters on perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*). Its phrasing is particularly harmonious and profound;
it should be studied with great care. (6)
Question: Although one contemplates other Buddhas without forming the notion of "other," one thereby enters the Dharma-gate of the non-duality of self and other.
Is this so, or not? Answer: When you attend to your parents, have you ever formed the thought: "These others are my parents"?
"Because my own body emerged from another, do I love and respect it? When I look toward my children and grandchildren, have I ever thought: 'They are my children and grandchildren;
their bodies emerged from me,' and thus feel intimacy toward them? He replied, "No. [The Master] said, "Precisely at that time, was the child's body present or not?
He replied, "Most often one is unaware of it. If one were aware of it, one would not be free [to act as one pleases]."
[The Master] said: "Since there is no longer any awakening [to duality], there is non-duality. Why then doubt the recollection of another Buddha? (7) Question:
When chanting the name, must one also contemplate the physical marks? Answer: The name inherently encompasses the marks, and the marks likewise include the name.

One does not invoke both separately; when one arrives, both arrive together. When you commonly see images of the Golden Body (Suvarṇakāya) extending its hand to guide others, your own mind naturally becomes obscured.

"Is it not the case that one calls out the name 'Amitābha Buddha'? He replied, "It is. [The Master] asked, "Even though you do not utter a sound, do you not seem to hear it yourself? He replied, "It is so.

"In that case," [the Master] said, "it is evident that names and forms are never separated from one another. It is like calling out from afar to an acquaintance: one need not deliberate upon their physical appearance;
yet when the intention reaches and the voice issues forth, one naturally feels a sense of intimacy. Therefore, one recites the Buddha's name."

This requires nothing more than making a sincere vow and counting the recitations on a rosary. (Regarding fixed daily recitations, it is better to have fewer than more; the essential point is to practice without interruption for the rest of one’s life.

I often see students who delight in speaking of lofty, superficial talk and refuse to count their recitations, eventually falling into neglect. This is something to be deeply cautioned against. Simply proceed with the recitation directly, regardless of whether the tone is high or low, slow or fast.
If you can truly maintain single-mindedness as if facing a strict master and receiving his personal instruction and supervision, then every single utterance will be like calling out to him.

O Compassionate Mother, if you exert your power to lift and guide me, then the two phrases from the "Chapter on Śrī-Ābhāsvara" regarding "the present and the future, one will certainly see the Buddha" will naturally become clear through internal examination; you will no longer need to seek news from others. It is asked:

The ancients considered the practice of visualization (*vipaśyanā*) to be the "concentrated good" (*samādhi-kuśala*) and the recitation of the name to be the "scattered good" (*vikṣepa-kuśala*). Why was visualization clearly regarded as more important?

It is said that the two terms "concentration" (*ding*) and "dispersion" (*san*) are not words of disparagement or praise; rather, they distinguish the ease or difficulty of the practice according to their respective modes of activity (*xingxiang*).

One must not misunderstand this. For those who practice visualization (*guan*), they must sit in silence with a clarified mind, the various sense faculties stilled, and enter the stages of realization in succession;

therefore, it is called "concentrated goodness. As for those who recite the Name, they are not restricted by walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, but may manifest [the practice] amidst all moving conditions.
Therefore, it is called "scattered goodness" (*prādeśika-kuśala*). Entering [the path] through gradual stages relies entirely on one's own power and is thus difficult;
realizing it immediately and bringing it forth relies exclusively on the power of others and is thus easy. The Original Vow of Amitābha lies solely in the invocation of the Name;

for this reason, although the Master of the Land (Śākyamuni) preached the *Contemplation Sūtra*, he ultimately concluded by returning to the Original Vow (as seen in detail in the preceding section). Master Shandao’s commentary on the *Contemplation Sūtra* emphasizes its power...

Having dispelled all delusions, he spent his entire life single-mindedly practicing the recitation of the Name and exhorted others on a vast scale. It is traditionally said that the Great Master was an emanation of Amitābha;
to this day, he is held in the highest esteem. Students should know where they ought to turn for guidance. (8)

Question: Every person possesses their own inherent nature (*svabhāva*). To rely exclusively on the power of another rather than one's own strength is precisely what is meant by "bending one’s own spiritual brilliance.
How can this be? Answer: When the ear hears sound and the eye sees form, is that not one's own inherent nature? [The questioner] says: It is.
The First Patriarch told King Hsien-chien (Vijaya) that it is indeed so. [The questioner] says: What the First Patriarch meant was that "that which is in the eye is called seeing."
Regarding these six instances of the character "equal" (等): Is this not the mind’s numinous knowing and numinous awakening? He said, “It is. [The Master] asked:

“If both light (with form) and darkness (without form) were absent, would the nature of seeing also be absent? If both clamor (with sound) and silence (without sound) were absent, would the nature of hearing also be absent?

(In ancient times, many wild Chan practitioners died at this point. As for the monks of recent times, they have never even dreamed of this—how can you speak of Chan? If one says it is absent, then the ears and eyes...
To be the same as wood or stone is to suppress one’s own spirit. If the Way is not non-existent, then where does it abide?

If you can leave behind sound and form in this very place, and turn your body and breathe forth to rescue your own spirit, you may be said to possess a measure of self-power; even so, you will still have rescued only half of it.
If you cannot do this, you should know what the ancient masters meant when they said: "Realizing through conditions is swift in its resonance; attaining directly from the essence..."
"Ceasing and resting gains power slowly. This single phrase of the Buddha’s name is truly like a thunderclap and a flash of lightning;

it causes all that is withered to sprout and all that is budding to fully reach fruition. Do not slander the power of *tariki* (other-power). (The two lines "Realizing through conditions" and "Attaining through reliance" specifically borrow the meaning of relying on external testimony to manifest *tariki*;

do not misunderstand this. If one can indeed recite directly from the outset, suddenly—as if seeing peach blossoms or hearing a painted horn—it will naturally be no hindrance to being an extraordinary master. Furthermore, one's faith in *tariki* will be such that even ten thousand oxen cannot pull it back. If you mistakenly treat this as the Zen school...)

Regarding the *huatou*: if you treat it as a mere broomstick or a piece of wood, you are profoundly mistaken; both gates are shattered. You must know that since this is the power of the Other (itara-bala), it can by no means be analyzed through one's own intellectual views (*jñāna-dṛṣṭi*).
When the karmic impulse and the occasion coincide, and the ten consciousnesses are exhausted, there is only the direct recitation [of the name] to bear the momentum. This alone is exactly right. (9)
Question: Amitābha’s original vow welcomes beings by means of their name; when sentient beings make a vow and recite the name, they are reborn there.

Since the vow and the practice correspond, there is no room for doubt in principle. However, those who have actually been reborn are extremely few, and there is little evidence to prove it. On what basis can one place one's trust? Answer:
A thousand doubts and ten thousand delusions all stem from failing to recognize the single thought-moment of the present. Now, the essence of the mind is quiescent illumination, a single reality.

It does not fall within any spatial location. Where there is thought, there is spatial location. The substance [of the mind] is like the mirror-essence; thought is like the mirror’s radiance. The various objects of thought are like shadows captured by that radiance.

This has already been briefly explained in the treatises (see the *綱宗* [Outline] and *雜說* [Miscellaneous Explanations] of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*). Since the substance of the mind is truly difficult to name or describe, I shall provisionally follow the traditional interpretations for the sake of clarity.

One should know that the substance of the mind does not possess a real material form. For instance, it is only when copper is refined and emits radiance that it is called a "mirror. If the radiance were to separate from the substance, it would become mere scrap metal. All such cases demonstrate that one must not cling to the literal words.
To further substantiate this with the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, let us examine its opening passage. At the very beginning of the scroll, it proclaims the single phrase:
"The Wondrously Profound, Total-Holding, Immovable Honored One. Here, the entire body and great function of the Buddha-nature are presented in their full integrity.

In the main text, the inquiry first seeks the mind through the "seven locations," which causes the practitioner to infer the fundamental essence by means of its reflections (all seven locations being merely reflections). Next, the vision is revealed through the "eight returns," which serves to...
It is to depart from shadows and directly recognize the fundamental substance. (All that is returned is shadow. This fundamental substance is true, eternal, and unchanging;

yet its function is infinitely manifold and inexhaustible. Therefore, it has no beginning and no end. The Buddha realized this as Amitāyus (Immeasurable Life). It has neither orientation nor aversion.
The Buddha realized this as Immeasurable Light (*Amitābha*). Although sentient beings are deluded and mistake their heads for reflections, they nonetheless wear their own heads upon them.

Therefore, within the single thought-moment of the present, whether above heaven or below earth, wherever one may go, there is nowhere it does not reach; for its essence is none other than Immeasurable Light.
Dying here and being born there, wandering through the cycle of karma without ceasing until now—this is because [its essence is Immeasurable Light].

The "Original" is none other than Amitāyus. Amida perceived this capacity and directly based his vows upon that very source, causing sentient beings to, in every thought-moment, relinquish all dharmas and simply recite His name; this is precisely to be free from all shadows in every thought-moment.
Yet one directly recognizes the fundamental substance (*dharmatā*). Thus, vow after vow corresponds to one another, like mirrors facing each other, their reflections swallowing one another’s light.
Self and other are distinct yet merged without interval; when this principle is manifest, all phenomena are contained therein.
Observe those in the world who, when their ears suddenly tingle or they suddenly sneeze, immediately say, "Who is thinking of me?"—thus, the hairs [of the body stand on end].
The *Shijing* states: "When one thinks of another, there is a sneeze. The Zheng Commentary says: "If you think of my heart in this way, I shall then sneeze.
Today, when common people sneeze, they say, "Someone is speaking of me. This is a remnant of ancient speech. Based on this, one can see that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are one.
They are universally of one essence; this has been known by all throughout antiquity and the present, yet people merely practice it without examining it.

(In ancient times there were no Buddhist teachings, yet the records state that when a king performed the *dì* sacrifice for his ancestor’s origin, Confucius said that one who understood the doctrine of *dì* could govern the world as easily as pointing at something in the palm of one's hand. What does this truly mean? Let readers reflect deeply upon it. Now, if ordinary minds correspond with one another, how much more so must it be with the Sage-mind?
If a single vow corresponds, how much more so must it be with two vows? If even distracted thoughts correspond, [how much more so must it be with pure resolve].
How much more so for one who maintains focused mindfulness! If even a fleeting thought corresponds [to the truth], how much more so constant mindfulness!

Furthermore, when ordinary people harbor thoughts of one another, they are precisely seeing reflections within the light, yet these still correspond; how much more so for one who directly recognizes the fundamental substance and does not forget it!
The principle is right before one’s eyes; why wait until after death? (10)
Question: You say that the mutual thoughts [of self and others] are like reflections in a mirror; this fills out the explanation.

Yet, if one were to regard one’s own liver and gallbladder as being as distant from each other as Chu and Yue, and view one’s sovereign and parents as mere passersby on the road, how could such a teaching be established? Answer: If all people are reflections, is one’s own body alone not a reflection?
It is precisely because one knows that the cycle of birth and death within a single lifetime is not the true self, that what one desires becomes more important than life itself. What...
Nothing is more wretched than death. Should one contravene this principle, one immediately loses their original mind.

Master Ziyu (Mencius) spoke of this long ago. (This is merely cited to prove that every person possesses a true self; it does not mean one has already transcended the Three Realms. Furthermore, within the Three Realms, the differences in status and rank are vast and incalculable.

If one examines the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, the *Biographies of Lay Practitioners*, various records of the Dharma-lamps, and the "Academies of Learning" for the Confucian scholars of the Song, Yuan, and Ming dynasties, one will see that those whose realization merely corresponds to the first and second dhyāna heavens are quite numerous. Indeed, unless one is a Bodhisattva dwelling in this [higher] station, it is difficult to guarantee [one's liberation].)

One shall not fall back. Those born in the Pure Land will perfectly realize the three non-regressions and, at the end of this single lifetime, reach the stage of the position immediately preceding Buddhahood (the *ekajātipratibaddha*). This is why, throughout thousands of sutras and treatises, they all point toward this as their ultimate goal. Furthermore, do you not observe the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*?
In the chapter on the "Five Torments and Five Burnings," the emphasis is placed upon social ethics and the principles of the royal law;

it provides repeated illustrations and parables for nearly two thousand words. I have already briefly explained this in the *Wǔliàngshòujīng gāngzōng*. If one can indeed practice according to these teachings, [one will attain the goal].
Dedicate all myriad virtues. Through long-term cultivation until they become pure and mature, one will naturally realize that "the present moment is it" and that "wherever one stands is the truth.
Only then, having shattered the mirror, can one meet the Buddha face-to-face. Since the prevalence of Chan studies, this scripture has been sealed away in the Great Canon;

even those who practice the recitation of the Buddha's name speak loftily of the ultimate mystery, yet regard this passage as belonging to the Hīnayāna, showing no inclination to even deign to read it.
All manner of doubts and difficulties are brought upon oneself; those who aspire to the Pure Land school should take this as a profound warning. (11) Question:
When one vows for rebirth, the primary retribution (*pratyaya-phala*) is clearly manifested. Are there also proofs for the various vows regarding the secondary environment (*niśraya-phala*)? Answer:
Where there is a body, there is a land (which is visible in the present). The environment-retribution arises from the primary-retribution and also transforms from the primary-retribution.

Whether one is wealthy or poor, noble or humble, their distinctions result in distinct environments. It is the same for the four lands and nine grades of the Land of Ultimate Bliss; however, the three lands are all inseparable from the Constant Quiescent Light Land—this must not be unknown.

Since those who attain rebirth must first discard this retribution-body before obtaining that [other] retribution-body, how could they possibly take up this retribution-land? This is used as a corroborative proof.

Regarding that land of recompense (*vipāka-kṣetra*): if one were to generally dissolve it back into its own nature (*svabhāva*), it would indiscriminately merge with the eternal truth (*dhruva-satya*).

Confused scholars have mistakenly interpreted this as a mere allegory (as noted in Master Lianchi’s *Shuchao*: "He has exerted his utmost effort and reached the pinnacle of his realization to encourage those at the beginning of their practice, yet there are many who misunderstand; this is why masters such as Ouyi have striven to correct them"). Mad Chan practitioners ultimately fall into the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*), which brings great harm while benefiting little;
this has already been clearly discerned in the *Xi-fang-he-lun*. Furthermore, when each point is compared [to other teachings], there must necessarily be...
What is the reason for this impasse? Why not immediately verify it through the vow made upon the invocation of his name? According to that Buddha’s original vow:
"In the worlds of the ten directions, if there are gods or humans who do not know my name, yet invoke my name, I shall not attain perfect enlightenment.
At the time when the golden man first entered the dream, the Middle Kingdom had certainly never heard of him. It was only during the period of the Han and Wei dynasties that—
This sutra was translated in successive stages, beginning earlier and continuing later, until it gradually circulated. At Donglin, it was championed, and the Dharma gate opened wide;

both monastics and laypeople turned their hearts toward it as swiftly as grass bending in the wind. however, the essential mind of the Buddhas and Patriarchs has clear textual evidence). One may read the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* of the Jin and Tang dynasties, the *Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs*, and...
