To the point where even those who do not consciously recite the Buddha’s name—when encountering circumstances of suffering or joy, or adversity and favor—unconsciously let out a cry, spontaneously calling out, "Amitābha Buddha" (as Bai Xiangshan already said). Regardless of whether one is noble or base, adult or child, it becomes as if it were their very nature.
It has been accomplished. Yet practitioners may even fail to recognize that the original teacher Śākyamuni and the future Maitreya are one;
how could this be a mere coincidence? How could this be a mere coincidence? The Buddha’s speech is never deceptive. Since the fulfillment of this vow is so manifest and evident, it is beyond doubt.

The remaining aspirations may be inferred; what need is there for further elaboration? (Nowadays, Buddhism has already spread throughout the various nations of the West. In the United States, there was a great virtuous man named Algot, who was originally a general. Because he harbored doubts regarding his own religion, he traveled extensively to seek out renowned masters.

Later, he encountered a Russian *upāsikā* [laywoman] who explained the essential points of the Buddha-dharma to him. He subsequently developed right faith, resigned from his official post, and devoted himself exclusively to cultivation. He promoted and exhorted others to follow the path.

Initially, the local officials and gentry viewed his departure as a cause for concern, but they soon observed that his teachings were superior and wholesome, and that the hearts of the people were drawn toward them. Consequently, they began to protect and support him with earnest care. Whenever a dharma-assembly was held to transmit the precepts, they provided respectful and diligent hospitality. Those who followed his faith increased daily until they numbered in the tens of millions.)

The scholars and commoners of various nations, both great and small, such as Great Britain and France, were all moved by his reputation and turned toward him with devotion. They received Ajahn [the Master] with due ceremony, requesting him to transmit the Dharma and bestow the precepts.

By common agreement, they established the banner of a Buddhist Convention and set up three or four hundred telegraph stations dedicated solely to discussing the Buddha-Dharma. Daily, they produced several hundred thousand sheets of paper for newspapers titled *Lingzhi Bao* (The Informative News). Thus, the Western nations’ approach to doctrine and principle—following human sentiments without clinging to fixed prejudices—is in profound accord with the intent of our own Three Dynasties’ eminent kings who observed the people to establish their teachings and governed for the sake of the people.

During the summer and autumn of the year Jichou (1909), Ajahn arrived in Shanghai from Japan to propagate the teachings. Xu Xixian and his son Jian went aboard his vessel one after another to meet him. Ajahn...

The official then asked, "Does the Great Emperor of your noble country believe in the Buddha-dharma? Xixian replied respectfully, "The successive sagely rulers have protected and upheld it; therefore, [the Emperor] said with joy, 'This is most excellent. He further inquired what the fundamental principle was. Xixian replied, "It simply requires faith in the Buddha and the recitation of his name; there is no other fundamental principle.

At present, we generally act in accordance with the hearts of the people, making the promotion of the orthodox and the expulsion of the heterodox our primary task. When he asked how the monastics of your noble country were, Xixian noted that they knew only how to build temples. Xixian wished to invite him to come ashore to preach the Dharma.

The official said that if there could be a thousand or ten thousand people gathered together to listen to the lectures, he would be very happy to comply. Fearing he might offend the taboos of the times, Xixian then desisted. Furthermore, there was the Western scholar Mr. Li Jiabai, named Timothy Richard, who was an Englishman.

He was proficient in both Chinese language and literature and was a believer in the Buddha-dharma; he was also an acquaintance of Master Xian’an. Several years ago, he specially invited the layman Yang Renshan to translate the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith) into English, intending to publish it to encourage and guide the scholars of his own country.

Mr. Li’s aspirations were truly great; out of compassion for our China, where no one was championing the True Teaching, he established the Shangxian Hall in the capital. Due to a lack of funds, he has now returned to his own country to solicit donations, vowing that the project will certainly succeed. From this, one can see the impartiality of truth and falsehood, which remains constant from heaven to earth.

Furthermore, it clearly demonstrates that the Original Vow of Amitābha, renowned throughout the ten directions, possesses verifiable reality. In several decades, the transformation by the Buddha will surely become unified under the public Dharma.

The strategy for pacifying the military that we have envisioned lies precisely here. The two masters, A-li (Amṛta) and Li (Nāgārjuna), were likely those who came again by virtue of their vows to respond to the prophecy of the Śarīra’s re-emergence. (12)

Question: "If the purity of the mind is the purity of the land, this is indeed the realm of wondrous existence (*miao-you*). Why, then, does the fundamental tenet (*gang-zong*) assert that the Pure Land is substantially real (*shi-you*)? Answer:
"If even a single hair’s breadth of a trace of the 'original' (*yuan*) remains in one's breast, one has already erroneously entered the eternally true Pure Land;
one is far removed from the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Jile-jingtu*). Question: "Why is that? Answer: "The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says: 'For example, suppose there were a person who wished to...'"
One may erect palaces and dwellings upon vacant ground as one pleases without hindrance, yet one can never achieve this in empty space.
It is precisely because the Bodhisattva wishes to bring sentient beings to maturity that he vows to take up a Buddha-land; that he vows to take up a Buddha-land is proof that it is not in the void.
This is clear evidence—how can you harbor doubts regarding the Western Pure Land? Furthermore, my son, when you now look upward and see the sky, have you ever...
One forms this thought: "Is there heaven here? When lifting the foot to place it upon the ground, one has never formed the thought: "Is there earth here? To which he replied: "No. He said:
"This is precisely what is called 'wondrous existence that is not existent,' and what is called 'the true mark that is markless.

(Do not, moreover, because of such statements, generally interpret the preceding discourse on "the very place where one stands is the truth" and "this very moment is it" as referring to a permanently real Pure Land. You should first consider: is this land itself wondrous existence?
Is this truly so? Even regarding what is before one's eyes, people remain deluded regarding the fundamental understanding; how much more so when it concerns that which lies far away in the West?

Our Original Teacher enumerated forty-eight vows, yet did not utter a single word to provide an analytical exposition [of them]. (I have often said that regarding the sutras on the original vows of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas for the salvation of sentient beings—such as those of Bhaisajyaguru, Ksitigarbha, and others—one may only interpret the text and explain the meaning.

These do not obstruct the conventional understanding and cannot be used for the contemplation of mind in accordance with principle; they would otherwise be indiscriminately categorized under the School of Emptiness. There is, however, a separate [method] for praising the merit and adornment of the Pure Land.
The passage "In the earth there is Buddha" repeats the character "you" (yǒu) seven times; this too merely points out names and appearances.

As for the jewel pond, the water of virtue, the rows of trees, and the gentle breeze—why can it alone not speak of the nature of water, the nature of wind, or the nature of true emptiness and the nature of awakening, as is done in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*?

Thus we know that the Pure Land school specifically teaches the cultivation of phenomena (*dharma*). Its single flavor and straightforward reality is precisely the pinnacle of compassion, reaching out to all capacities through its manifold manifestations.

Whether one’s insight is shallow or deep depends on the person, not on the objective realm. (For this very reason, while all equally realize the *sāmbhogakāya* land of tranquil light, there are distinctions of excellence among the four lands and gradations among the nine grades.

If everything were to correspond exactly to the ultimate principle, it would conversely become a mere phenomenon of conditioned appearance. Try examining the *Smaller Sukhāvatī-vyūha Sūtra*; regarding the Dharma-preaching by the miraculous birds, it specifically provides a detailed analysis of the evil realms.
The reality of these [realms] is non-existent; their fundamental basis lies in the Four Heavenly Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and so forth. Upon what do they depend for their abiding?
It was specifically through Ānanda posing a question that it was stated, "I do not doubt this, but I do so for the sake of future sentient beings, to eliminate their doubts.

If readers at such points can immediately transcend the words while remaining within them, and if their vision shines forth perfectly, then they will attain realization regarding the Pure Land school.

"More than half [of the work] has been completed. (Observing the statement in the *Sūtra* that "the mind creates the mind," the commentaries explain this by establishing the meaning of entrusting [the mind] to the external; thus, the two phrases for the contemplation of "mind-only" are established. This is the ultimate clarity regarding the suffering of the mind.

Yet, readers still mistakenly interpret this as meaning there is no Pure Land at all. Therefore, in the *Gangzong*, the meaning of "this" is analyzed in detail, first concluding with the two phrases: "If it were not real, even though one contemplates it, nothing would be accomplished. I hope that readers will reflect deeply upon this. Since the prevalence of Western learning, there have been many Buddhist texts sufficient to provide corroboration.

For instance, when astronomers calculate the stars and moon, they all depict the shapes of mountains, rivers, and the great earth, which resembles this globe. This globe exists within the vast emptiness of space and is itself but a single star among the many wandering celestial bodies.)

They revolve daily. Each of these fixed stars also acts as a sun, around which there are likewise countless revolving planets, equal in scale to these solar systems; however, they are so distant that they cannot all be seen. Furthermore, it is said that the two planets Venus and Mercury have no accompanying moons.
Mars has two moons; Jupiter has four; Saturn has eight; Uranus also has four; and Neptune has one. All these moons revolve around their respective planets, no differently than the moon of the Earth.

According to this, it can be corroborated with the Buddha’s teaching of the world-system of ten billion suns and moons. It further states that Saturn is most extraordinary, possessing a luminous ring around its body divided into three layers, broad, level, and extremely vast; the diameter of the space outside this ring is over five million one hundred thousand *li*.

Examining this halo, it is like a mass of clouds that does not disperse; this can be corroborated by the Buddha’s teaching regarding the distinction between the gods who dwell on earth and those who dwell in the clouds. Furthermore, it is said that all moving and stationary beings existing upon other celestial bodies must necessarily differ from those on Earth for three reasons:
first, the amount of solar light and heat they receive differs; second, the magnitude of their gravitational pull differs; and third, the density of their physical substance differs.

This can be corroborated by the Buddha’s teaching that the adornments and Buddha-activities of the various Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions are each uniquely superior and distinct. From these points above, it is evident that space is inexhaustible and worlds are inexhaustible; the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss lies beyond the trichiliocosm.

The celestial realms truly possess sacred lands, adorned with various meritorious virtues; yet these do not lie outside the inconceivable mind and the essence of awakening of sentient beings. Those who have traditionally discussed the Pure Land school often claim that this [Pure Land] belongs solely to this world, thereby becoming biased toward the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and falling into the error of asserting that while the principle exists, the phenomena do not. This is a grave mistake. (13)

Question: The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states that if a world were truly existent, it would be a "unified mark" (*ekapiṇḍalakṣaṇa*). Pure Lands are precisely the opposite of such marks; why is this? Answer:
The Pure Land school and the Emptiness school stand in opposition to one another; this has been detailed in the fundamental principles of their respective teaching systems (*dharmamukha*).
Their opposition serves precisely to bring about mutual completion. This is evident from the very opening of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, as has already been cited above.

This has been realized. When the numinous light shines alone, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects, not a single dharma confronts the mind, and neither knowledge nor views are established.
Yet, sentient beings perceive a realm of form when the eye encounters color, and perceive a realm of sound when the ear encounters sound;

they grasp at appearances and engage in discrimination, their emotional attachments being so deep and heavy that there is no way to escape birth and death. (These are words from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, translated by the Song dynasty) — therefore, the School of Emptiness was taught.
In various sutras, the phrase "removing names and dispelling appearances" leads back to the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).

The meaning of these two phrases is like saying that when one person awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the worlds of the ten directions immediately dissolve and vanish; this is spoken from the perspective of an individual’s own realization.

How could it mean that everything truly vanishes into nothingness? This sutra establishes its beginning with non-self (*anātman*) and extends it to the absence of the four marks (*catur-nimitta*). From...

From beginning to end, by means of the two meanings of "that which is not" and "name," he speaks accordingly and sweeps away accordingly, reaching the ultimate point where there is neither attainment nor speech.
Now, having already stated that there is no attainment, he further states that by practicing all wholesome dharmas without self, person, sentient being, or life-span, one immediately attains Bodhi.
Having already stated that there is no dharma that can be taught, he further states regarding the Dharma...

He speaks of the characteristic of cessation, yet does not say that the characteristic of permanence is not spoken of. If that is so, then ultimately, how should one abide? How should one subdue [the mind]?
At the end, he reveals the essential purport, saying: "Regarding all dharmas, one should know them thus, see them thus, and believe and understand them thus;
do not give rise to the notion of dharmas. This is what is meant by "abiding thus" and "subduing thus."
This is perfectly clear. The Pure Land school is established precisely from this point. Those who expound the Pure Land and those who cultivate the Pure Land should all enter through this gateway;

do not shift from your fundamental position. (Do not see such a statement and immediately claim that the Pure Land school does not grasp at signs. One must know that as soon as one clings to even a single thought of "non-grasping," that is itself a shifting of the fundamental position—be most careful, be most careful!
My own deep faith in the Pure Land school was truly gained through the power of these few sentences; I venture to bring them forth here.
To share this with all those of clear vision in every direction. (14) Question:
Since both good and evil arise from the perceptions of the mind, and one already knows that their nature is empty, what is the use of practicing good? Answer:

Practicing good is precisely for the sake of realizing the emptiness of nature; one must not merely know its explanation. The Golden Sūtra states that practicing the four immeasurables is itself [the realization of emptiness].

This principle is as follows: those who cling to the view of self are called ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Those who merely empty the view of self are called followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

Those who further empty the view of phenomena (*dharmadṛṣṭi*) are called followers of the Mahāyāna. When both views are empty, and even the emptiness of both is itself empty, this is called the Supreme Vehicle (*anuttarayāna*).
These are all merely names. Regarding their fundamental essence, which is empty by nature, there is in reality not even a hair’s breadth of gain or loss.

Thus, the *Zongjing lu* quotes from a sutra (the specific sutra is not recorded): "The self-nature is originally without stinginess or greed; accordingly, one practices the *dāna-pāramitā* (translated here as 'generosity').
The self-nature is originally without deviance or delusion; accordingly, one practices the *śīla-pāramitā* (translated here as 'precepts'). The self-nature...
By nature, there is originally no anger; one accordingly practices the pāramitā of kṣānti (translated as "patience"). By nature, there is originally no indolence;
one accordingly practices the pāramitā of vīrya (translated as "diligence"). By nature, there is originally no distraction;
one accordingly practices the pāramitā of dhyāna (translated as "meditative concentration"). By nature, there is originally no delusion; one accordingly practices the pāramitā of pra... [prajñā].

If [it refers to] the *prajñāpāramitā* (translated as "wisdom"), then within the teachings, the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate natures are established as the three self-natures (*trisvabhāva*). In reality, however, these are the *karmic consciousness*. To speak by tracing them back to their source, in all such instances:

One must examine and distinguish these matters thoroughly before one can understand them; this very passage is a prime example. It correctly explains that emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) means that the six perfections, such as giving (*dāna*), are merely designated as "good" in contrast to evil, yet they too are fundamentally non-existent.

Mencius did not refute the error of Gaozi’s old doctrine that there is neither good nor evil; he simply stated, "If we consider their emotional nature (*qíng*), it is capable of being made good. Furthermore, in other chapters where he speaks of the goodness of human nature, he frequently points to the mind of compassion (*cèyǐn*) and so forth. This is precisely because the state prior to "humanity being born into stillness" cannot be designated by the names of good or evil.

The single phrase, "That which is desirable is good," is a truly profound statement; it clearly begins from the perspective of emotional nature (*qíng*). The Song Confucians dragged this into the *Appended Judgments* of the *Book of Changes* and the *Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate* (*Tàijí tú*), claiming that because emotional nature can be made good, one sees that the nature itself is fundamentally good. They have completely missed the point.

(Regarding the intent of Mencius, I have discussed it elsewhere. All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas encompass all virtues within these six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) to achieve the supreme wisdom of the supramundane world.
They benefit themselves and others; all evils are utterly eliminated, yet they do not establish "good" for themselves.

It is like using a wedge to extract another wedge: once the former wedge has departed, how could the latter remain? Thus, we know that cultivation arising in accordance with one's nature is itself non-action.

Cultivate, cultivate! Through cultivation, one realizes the nature; this is precisely "realization through non-realization. The dedication of all wholesome deeds in the Pure Land school is likewise so.
When worldly people hear it said that one should cultivate goodness, they become attached to conditioned, minor virtues;

when they hear it said that the nature is empty, they fall into a state of vacuous, insentient emptiness. Thus they lose both. Yet the former loss is still beneficial for the realms of humans and devas, whereas the latter loss is great.
Because it destroys worldly appearances, the Pure Land school exclusively emphasizes the cultivation of phenomena. For forty-nine years, [the Buddha] taught with fervent and uninterrupted diligence;

it was only at the very end that the Chan school finally brought forth its core teaching. This was truly out of concern for its perilous and difficult nature. Thus, one can perceive the original intent of his transcendence from the world.
Observing that the capacities of sentient beings have matured, he manifests birth; it is certain that this is not solely for the sake of a single cycle of birth and death.
This has already been briefly stated in the "Summary of the Essential Principles" and the "Miscellaneous Explanations. (15)

Question: Since both involve single-minded, exclusive mindfulness and the dedication of the myriad practices toward rebirth, why is it that rebirth in the Upper Grade belongs specifically to śramaṇas?
Answer: This principle has already been briefly discussed previously. To revere the Buddha is like revering a Confucian scholar.
Although there are many different classes and types in the world, the scholar is the foremost among the four occupations; for his person is enrolled in the ranks of the academy.

This is the Confucian tradition. One who has thoroughly investigated the Way that penetrates Heaven, Earth, and humanity is called a Ru (Confucian). Such individuals are one in ten thousand. How could the meager pursuit of official degrees through the civil service examinations ever be deemed worthy of this?

According to the Buddhist precepts, those wishing to leave the household life must first receive the five precepts for lay practitioners; only when they are able to maintain them perfectly may they proceed.

Thereafter, having petitioned the sovereign and one’s parents, and down to one’s wife, children, and servants, once all have granted their permission, one may receive the tonsure and advance to the śrāmaṇera precepts.

After many years of rigorous purification, one advances again to the bhikṣu precepts. Only after another many years of rigorous purification does one finally attain the full and perfect bodhisattva mahā-śīla.

Even then, one must continue to study until mastery is achieved regarding what is permitted and what is prohibited, as well as the maintenance and violation of the precepts. Thus is the perfection [of the training].

Only when one has attained unimpeded mastery can one then guide disciples and lead a community, being entitled to the title of *śramaṇa*. Therefore, a single ordination platform may accept only three persons;

to exceed this limit is to cause the dharma to become diluted. Although one might seek [ordination] and yet fail to obtain the precepts, one must be able to traverse the most rigorous path before one does not fail the most generous span of time.
(One must not maintain a wife or children, and must minimize worldly toil. One must be able to find sweetness in the most frugal food.
"Eating but one meal at midday and staying but one night under a tree" truly lives up to the exalted reputation of being "the Teacher of Gods and Humans.

If this is indeed so, then the Four Great Vows will surely be fulfilled; how could they not be held in high esteem? The removal of hair and beard is intended to prevent the confusion of social interactions;

it is certainly not for the sake of valuing a change of dress or the disfigurement of one's appearance. When Vimalakīrti manifested illness, all the great disciples each declined the honor [of visiting him].
I cannot bear to go and inquire further. It can be known that the Buddha-way is impartial, making no distinction between the monastic and the lay.

Those who study Buddhism do not deeply contemplate the original intent of the Buddha’s regulations; seeing only praise for leaving the household life, they consequently fixate exclusively upon the hair on their heads.

Those who have left the household life, though they be like mute sheep or wild foxes, are singularly trusted; those remaining in the household, though they be true dragons or complete elephants, are singularly doubted.

Buddhist scriptures, though they be minor works on cause and effect, are held in high esteem; Confucian texts, though they be the great classics of the *Analects* and *Mencius*, are treated with neglect.
It is no wonder that this invites slander and ridicule, and that such decline and ruin can no longer be rectified. Alas! (From the "Discourse on the Selection of Talent" in the *Wangzhi*).

"Guan Zhong gathered his followers and lived in a community; this was the educational system of the Eastern Zhou. Confucius and Mencius traveled about seeking food for their livelihood; these were all exceptional measures adopted because the age had declined and the Way had become obscure. Yet even among readers today, none seem to realize this—how lamentable! (16)

Question: If one practices mindfulness of the Buddha and cultivates goodness, yet delusive thoughts (*vikalpa*) are not eliminated, can one still attain rebirth [in the Pure Land]? Answer: One will certainly attain rebirth; delusive thoughts are not a cause for concern.
The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Āryāvaivartikacakrasamādhisūtra*) says: "At all times, do not give rise to delusive thoughts; yet do not extinguish the various delusive minds.
Abide within the realm of delusive objects without adding further cognition; and within this state of non-cognition, do not..."
Discerning Reality: "My son, what do you now consider to be deluded thought? He replied, "When reciting the Buddha's name, calculating other matters.

[The Master] said, "This, however, is precisely the arising of deluded thought. The fault lies in a lack of awareness. (As an ancient worthy said: "I am not afraid of thoughts arising; I only fear that awakening is late. Once there is awareness, it is immediately eliminated.

There is no need for further removal; that is to say, knowing that it is an illusion is itself liberation, requiring no expedient means. To be free from illusion is itself awakening, without any gradual stages.

Even if one repeatedly awakens and repeatedly gives rise [to thoughts], and repeatedly gives rise and repeatedly awakens, as long as the mindfulness of the Buddha is uninterrupted, one will in total attain rebirth in the Pure Land.

Why is this? If one contemplates from the perspective of the essence of awakening (*bodhi*), all thoughts are delusions. According to the doctrinal principles of the Pure Teaching, from the very first generation of the mind of enlightenment, one transcends the Two Vehicles and proceeds directly toward the Three Stages of Worthies (*śaikṣa*).

(The *Yaojie* states that "directly transcending" refers to the forty-one stages; this is the ultimate explanation. Here, however, we speak from the perspective of the stage of learning for ordinary beings.

Without applying further discernment regarding what is delusory and what is non-delusory, one is equal to Perfect Awakening (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). If one contemplates from the perspective of the Dharma-gate, the arising of every thought to recite the Buddha’s name is precisely to follow [the path].
It accords with the nature of awakening; relying upon external objects, it is fully manifested. Delusion has no self-substance; it exists only because of non-awakening.
Try, when reciting the Buddha’s name, to intentionally give rise to delusion—you will certainly be unable to do so, while the Buddha’s name in your mouth becomes increasingly clear.

It can be seen that this is simply a single awakening, with no further place for arising. Furthermore, after finishing the recitation of the Buddha’s name, reflect back on what you have falsely conjured: what is it?
Names and forms are inevitably mostly obscure and utterly without influence, whereas the names of the Buddhas one recollects can be counted one by one;

if one reflects briefly upon them, their profound stillness is as if present before one. Thus it is evident that within right mindfulness, every phrase and every sound truly possesses efficacious power.
Fundamentally, the real is not in opposition to the delusory such that they stand as two; what illness could there be? (17) Question:

If one does not give rise to thoughts, yet when external conditions encounter the senses, it is impossible not to do so. What is to be done? Answer: When thoughts arise, bring them to mind as the Buddha. As long as there is thought, there is a body.
If the view of a self-body is not yet forgotten, one will generally perceive and receive sensory contacts. However, one must simply not lose the correctness [of mindfulness].
Mindfulness is itself the perfect clarity of concentration and wisdom; therefore, students should examine themselves within.
When encountering sudden circumstances of suffering or joy, adversity or favor, if the name of the Buddha first arises in the mind, one will maintain firm grasp at the moment of death.

It is simply right here; there is no need to seek profound theories or obstruct those of middling or inferior capacity. (One must say that at the moment of death, there is naturally a grasp for that which cannot be grasped.)

One would then lose the fundamental intent of the Dharma-gate. Dongpo’s words at the time of his death were originally not incorrect; he was certainly destined for rebirth in the Pure Land. It is only because he manifested signs of cleverness that students remain skeptical to this day.

If one were to say, as Master Yin Shilu did, "There are neither ghosts nor spirits, and there is no terror," then one would be truly mistaken. Generally speaking, when Confucians study Chan, they often fall into the realms of the heavens of non-perception or the formless realm. Had there been a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) at that time, it would have sufficed to ask him a single question: "Where are you? This would have guaranteed that Dongpo would recognize [his own state]. He said:
"There are no external conditions, yet it is beyond the reach of ordinary thought. Having long since forgotten the realm due to its distance, it suddenly [manifests]..."
"It appears before me. What can be done about it? [The Master] said: "This is the shadow of the six sense-objects within the eighth consciousness since beginningless time.
When the primary cause becomes clear and still, light is produced; it occasionally flows forth, arising and ceasing according to the moment.

It is truly not worth regarding as a fault. However, upon reaching this state, one enters a slight stupor. Worldly people often become greedily attached to it, thinking that the body and its environment are gradually being forgotten."
In truth, this is not permissible; you must urgently rouse your spirit. It is better to allow it to gradually dissipate than to remain thus. Why?

The Great Radiance of Spiritual Brilliance unifies both capacities into a single essence. (Whether one’s physical constitution is wise or foolish, sharp or dull, these are the internal manifestations of this light;

Therefore, its power and function are inconceivable. (That which is "inconceivable" is where the movements of the mind cease; that which is "inexpressible" is where the path of language is cut off. It surpasses all light. (Just as the light of a mirror leaves no trace, this refers to the lingering shadows of external objects; to remember and maintain them without forgetting is the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna*.

I once, during the middle of the night, was recollecting the Buddha while walking in circumambulation around my room. Suddenly, I saw the stars and moon directly above me, bright and pure. At that time, I did not know where my own eyes were located, nor did I perceive anything as strange. After a brief moment, I became aware of it, and it immediately vanished. The various Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions are all sustained by the power of this light, while its own essence remains eternally quiescent. When a person is...

In the midst of the intersection of the vital energies (*qi*), when the energies gather, there is life; when the energies disperse, there is death. This present moment of thought is the illumination of this one great spiritual light (*mahā-prabhā*);

For *qi* possesses material points, and thus has aggregation and dispersion; the numinous light, however, is a complete and unified whole. It merges with...
They transform through their identity. The vital energy (qi) circulates within the radiant light, like mist and smoke dispersing within sunlight;
according to whether it is sparse or dense, it even undergoes momentary change and extinction, yet it never departs from the light, nor does the light ever shift.

In the intervals between every grain of sediment, there is nothing but water. Depending on the weight of their substance, they either sink or float, yet the water itself never moves.

Ordinary people, throughout their entire lives, remain mired in agitation, clinging to this body—a mere provisional combination of the four great elements—as being the self (the seventh manas-vijñāna).

It illuminates the great earth (a metaphor for the eighth consciousness). When one reflects it with a mirror and turns it by hand (dissolving the characteristics of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses), its shimmering reflection appears within the room.
One mistakes this for the real sun, and thus this single great spiritual light transforms into the ignorance of karmic consciousness (*avidyā-karma-vijñāna*).

Those who practice the mindfulness of the Buddha and seek rebirth in the Western Pure Land—regardless of whether they understand their own conscious nature or not, and regardless of the extent of their deluded thoughts—will certainly attain rebirth provided they can make a sincere vow, establish a fixed schedule for practice, and maintain it without interruption throughout their lives. Why is this?
It is like two people who both mistakenly perceive the sun as being near; yet, while one uses a concave mirror to reflect its light back [to see it clearly], the other does not.

A mirror (a metaphor for the vow) is placed facing the sun (the spiritual light, which is the Buddha of self-nature; one must know that the mirror and the sun are originally one, yet it cannot be said otherwise). It is positioned toward the west.
From time to time, its focus is adjusted to concentrate the light (a metaphor for mindfulness). A moxa stick is held beneath it (a metaphor for the actual reality of the adornments of the Pure Land).

Yet, between the sun and the mirror, there is always a dense, misty haze that never ceases (a metaphor for the vital breath and deluded thoughts; in truth, it is one's own body that obstructs the space between them). Therefore—

For those whose self-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is light, it is easier to attain power. The sunlight cannot penetrate completely; at the moment of death, as the breath gradually fades and the smoke and mist gradually dissipate, the present single thought-moment remains (this is the sunlight).
The Buddha-body immediately manifests within the mirror (because my vow is identical to the Buddha’s vow).

"Purified light" refers to the attainment of the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*), which ultimately realizes the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*); this is precisely what it means to be reborn following the Buddha.

their lifting and lowering are simultaneous. Therefore it is said: "If born, one is certainly born; if departing, one truly does not depart. (These are the words of Chan Master Tianru.

As for this person: at the time of death, they see the Buddha as if seeing him in a dream; though their mouth cannot speak, in their heart there is a mingling of shame, regret, and joy.
This can be taken as proof. (23)
Question: Is the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) not perhaps the same as the body in a dream? Answer: They are vastly different.

Dreams are of many kinds (the three types governed by the *Taishi* of the *Zhouguan* serve as the framework; the six types governed by the *Gumeng* serve as the details). Tracing them back to their source, they are all movements of the numinous light and the natural boundary (*tian-ni*). Therefore, the ancients valued them greatly, and the Buddhist tradition values them as well.
Ultimately, they do not transcend the silent illumination of the single thought-moment of the present; thus, they cannot emit vital energy (*qi*) or emerge [from the body].
As for sound: since one is mindful that it is originally detached from the breath, the moment sound is produced, it becomes mere idle chatter.

Although the mind-born body is fundamentally identical to a single thought, the spiritual radiance coalesces to form a shape, like the flame of a lamp; it clearly possesses a physical substance, sound, and respiration.

Although the teachings frequently speak of luminosity, they never speak of the vital air (except for a single instance in the *Wǔjiàoyí* composed by later generations, which cites the Zhuangzi’s theory of "borrowing the *dū* [governor] as the scripture," yet even this record does not [affirm it]).

Therefore it is said: "The alternation of one yin and one yang constitutes the Way. Yang is the light that is originally present; yin is the qi that arises subsequently. (Therefore, women...)

The substances and physical forms of things in this world are all formed by the condensation of qi; therefore, when alchemists transform them, they all return to being qi.

they are precisely the proportions of the various objects that adorn that land. A person dwelling within the great radiance throughout their entire life would be unable to see them.
As for those who see only the sunlight, it is like being in broad daylight;

yet if one were to light a great candle inside a room and stand for a long time in the sunlight before entering that room, one's vision would become completely dark, unable to perceive a single thing, and unable to take even a single step.

As for those with superior visual acuity, they may be able to see the flame of a candle, yet they cannot distinguish its distance, direction, or location. The chamber is analogous to the physical body.

It is like a solitary lamp beneath the sun: its illuminating function is rendered ineffective. All teachings arise from the existence of a world.

When Amitābha, during his stage of practice as a bodhisattva, was the minister Ratnākara and vowed to attain a pure land (as seen in the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra*), it was like people of the West today seeking out sand islands in the ocean to clear land for settlement. That land possesses its own...

Because its seed is pure, it is taken as the means to purify the Buddha-land. Furthermore, it encompasses the pure practices of two hundred and ten billion lands.
And thus he adorns it. This is what is meant by the saying: "As his mind is pure, so is the Buddha-land pure"; it is not that there is nothingness or emptiness.
The Bhikṣu Dharmākara manifested himself in this land, left his country to renounce the world, and attained fruition in that land.
It is like when Śākyamuni dwelt in the world: ascending to the Tuṣita, Trāyastriṃśa, and Mahesvara heavens to preach the Dharma was an occurrence within meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
His manifesting in the royal palace to preach the *Amitābha Sūtra*, traversing the void, and returning to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain were all instances of his physical body (*rūpakāya*) coming and going.

their accumulated years naturally possess varying lengths. All such varieties do not transcend the commonality of human sentiment and the principles of affairs; regarding the Buddha—
From the perspective of its ultimate nature, it is called "wondrous function without effort. Yet in reality, one must still move one's hands and feet;

It is because the view of the body and the view of phenomena are not empty.
Śākyamuni preached various Mahāyāna sūtras, employing manifold methods of refinement to lead people to realize that the nature of the mind is originally vast, sovereign, and eternally indestructible.

Yet, he invariably pointed toward the Pure Land as the ultimate destination because this world is subject to formation and must inevitably undergo destruction—just as the "kalpa-ashes" were found in the Kunming Pool during the Han dynasty, and as Westerners have opened ancient tombs to find soil formed by the accumulation of shells and insects.

Among the various planets, there are many that existed in antiquity but no longer exist today (this is especially clear evidence). Once one is reborn in that land, one returns to the original nature of one's fundamental radiance, which never changes.

Therefore, while the various sutras universally exhort rebirth, they do so using only ordinary language, referring to the names and characteristics of its adornments without offering a single word of detailed explanation.
This is like encouraging someone to move residence; one simply describes what a certain place is like.
Victory is thereby attained. Yet, if one insists on deeply investigating how this comes to be, then no matter what object one takes up and pursues to the limit, nothing can ever be fully understood.
It is like the Confucian texts stating that "Heaven opened at Zi and Earth was laid out at Chou.
Did humans open it or did humans lay it out? Was it opened by itself or laid out by itself? Furthermore, from where do the two characters *zi* and *chou* themselves come? Who...?

"From this, one knows it. (The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that the world arises from the movement of the very first thought-moment. Commentators say that once a person has moved their mind in such a way, they are not permitted to investigate further.

This is precisely what constitutes "skillful understanding. All of these are later explanations of the Perfect and the Sublime; they are various ingenious views that constitute obstacles to the truth.
Indeed, even Śākyamuni could not have anticipated them. (24)

Question: Regarding the Pure Land school, you may be said to have contemplated it deeply and expressed it exhaustively. Yet, why do you consider this work to consist of dead words? Answer: Speech itself has no depth or shallowness;
depth or shallowness resides in the listener’s reception of the words. Therefore, I venture to express my thoughts fully.
The mind attains depths and shallowness; only the mind itself knows this. Your mind is not my mind, and thus you do not know the shallowness of mine while seeking the depth of mine.
Though I may employ a thousand or ten thousand words to explain myself, my inability to be deep remains;

you will ultimately regard me as one who finds depth unworthy of pursuit and lacks the desire for it. Why is this? The measure of depth and shallowness arises from the capacity [of the mind]. It does not—
Its measure can never be seen. Allow me to speak with you regarding this measure. As stated in the *Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta* of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, concerning the quantity known by the Tathāgata:
one begins with one hundred *lakṣas* (some say "hundred million," some say "ten thousand";

here we follow the latter), and multiplies it successively by itself until the one hundred and twenty-second stage. (In the commentaries, the figure of one hundred and twenty-four is given because it includes the two preceding numbers—the initial *lakṣa* and the *koṭi*—in the calculation.)
...it becomes unspeakably unspeakable times ten million. It stops abruptly. From beginning to end, it has a numerical count but no [fixed] meaning.

That the Original Teacher opened his mouth and spoke this chapter immediately was to clarify each and every cultivation.
Realization: all these arise from the essence to manifest as function. Furthermore, while reading the *Guǎnzǐ*, I learned that the square arises from the circle, and the circle arises from the mind.

If one calculates this by means of points, lines, surfaces, and volumes: with one hundred units for each of the vertical and horizontal sides, the area is ten thousand and the volume is one million, forming a cubic body.

this demonstrates that a single point universally possesses ten elemental gates (*daśadhātu*), and these tens are inexhaustible. This is all that can be known.
Although he had investigated the principle of emptiness, he was ultimately unable to enter into the phenomenal aspects of the one hundred and twenty-two successive stages of the self-vehicle.

After specializing in his studies for a long time, he finally realized that the key to this chapter lies in the single character "knowledge" (知). This character "knowledge" refers to the luminous, self-natured awareness and illumination, which is entirely direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Its "substance" (*śarīra*) refers to the spatial dimensions reached by the light of the mind; this is what is meant by "measure" (*pramāṇa*). (The *Shuchao* states that its primary thesis is to manifest the limits of its virtues by means of numbers; this is correct.

It uses the two characters "limit" (*fenqi*) to explain the character "measure," bringing it to the utmost clarity. The mind is fundamentally immeasurable and its entire substance is true emptiness; this is the "Dharma-realm of Principle" (*li-fajie*).

there is already clear evidence of this. There are two proofs for this.

One forms this thought: it is not immediately present as even a single momentary thought, yet it is not separate from even a single momentary thought.

There are three ways of realization regarding the various dharma-gates of the sūtras: they do not go beyond the elimination of names and the dispatching of signs. the intent of the various *dharma*-gates in the sutras is to illustrate the capacity of the vessel. Therefore, one must empty out every grain of rice before the full measure can be revealed.

In the *dharma*-gate of the Pure Land, it is by means of the rice filling the vessel to the brim that the full measure of the capacity is realized through actual proof. Upon seeing the rice, one knows it.
Not relying on calculation, this knowledge of all sutras serves precisely to eliminate [delusions] for the sake of establishing the Pure Land;

it is like emptying out grains of rice to reveal the total quantity, or seeking the capacity of a container to measure the grains of rice. (To preach the Dharma of True Emptiness with great eloquence:

Its realization is fourfold:

It does not go beyond the sense organs and their objects; furthermore, it speaks only of phenomena (*vastu*). Alas, sentient beings have long cultivated habits of delusion, which take desire as their root, causing them to be driven by names and forms. Thereupon, Amitābha, with a heart of ultimate compassion, accords with the nature of their illness and provides medicine through skillful means. That is to say:

Let that mind of desire fill the ocean of my vows; in turn, let the ocean of my vows encompass that mind of desire, so that this entire nature of manifestation and fulfillment may be fully realized as practice. Thus, essence and function are revealed face-to-face.

It does not depend on verbal expression. Therefore, within the state where purity and defilement, suffering and pleasure are one and the same, it specifically overturns the deep to manifest the shallow, discriminating between this and that:
returning purity to its purity, defilement to its defilement, pleasure to its pleasure, and suffering to its suffering (just as turbid water and clear water are both equally pure).
This precisely reveals the functioning of this single thought-moment: that from the entirety of the Real, delusion arises, yet even so, everything is already fully accomplished; everything...
It is fully complete, transcending all dependence and lacking any counterpart—how much more so in its fundamental essence! Therefore, to speak of "principle" or "nature" becomes redundant speech;

whereas to speak of "phenomena" or "cultivation" is precisely not outside the scope of reality. This is because sentient beings are, within their own present bodies, already fully manifest as the complete and perfect sentient beings.
It is like the treasury and storehouses of a wealthy family: they are already fully present and complete, with their records clearly and definitively established.
