I have specifically brought forth this principle so that you may know whether or not rebirth is attained depends upon the individual’s silent self-examination amidst their thoughts and deliberations.
It is unnecessary to calculate how things will be at the moment of death; rather, as for those around them—
In examining one’s lifelong conduct and practice, one must not take the state at the moment of death as the definitive criterion.
There is great confusion and error in this regard, and it bears significant relation to worldly conventions. A rough distinction of the grades is provided above;
I await correction from those with clear vision.
The five treatises composed within the Dharma Hall have been widely transmitted and copied; however, they have only undergone a single round of critical annotation by my senior friend, Li Xiangyan.
I have now transcribed them as they were. While I am aware that such excessive praise will surely incur the world’s censure, I could not help but disregard my own concerns.
This is not only because those capable of true understanding are rare, but because I could not bear to abandon these works.
In recent times, the Chan school has been swept away, leaving nothing left to discuss; yet the Pure Land school has likewise suffered considerable confusion and error.
Demonic followers have taken advantage of these gaps, and the disorder of their original intent has become increasingly deep-seated.

Local scholars of little learning remain entirely unaware of the state’s sincere intention to protect and sustain [the Dharma] over the past two hundred-odd years, nor do they understand the developments in our own region in recent times, such as those at Peng...

If even those gentlemen alone, who possess deep intentions for conversion according to the occasion, instead further exert their bureaucratic airs—enclosing temple lands within the Fengshan Academy, strictly forbidding the consumption of vegetarian food, and coercing the destitute masses into a heterodox teaching—the circumstances are truly appalling and painful.
I have now briefly set these forth in the "Song for Awakening the Deluded"; those with a discerning heart should examine them for themselves.

I have realized this. After this treatise was published, the layman Xi Anxu read the commentary until he reached the two phrases, "The path for turning back is cut off" and "Calling out to Heaven from on high.
He bowed his head toward the north, weeping so bitterly that he lost his voice. He showed it to Master Li, who annotated it as follows:
"In the vastness of the world, there must surely be scholars of great erudition and eminent talent who understand this."
Returning by virtue of his vows, he is one who can truly bear this appraisal. It is my wish that throughout all my future lives, I may sacrifice my body as an offering to him.
Recorded in the winter of the Dingyou year.

In the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*, Śākyamuni and Amitābha speak in two successive passages regarding those who attain rebirth: they state that rebirth is granted to all sentient beings, with the sole exception of those who commit the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) or slander the true Dharma.

However, the *Contemplation Sūtra* states that those of the lowest of the low grade are reborn despite having committed the five heinous crimes and slandering the Dharma, and being possessed of all manner of evils.

"Excellent. One who should have fallen into the evil realms, at the moment of death, encounters a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who provides various forms of consolation and instructs them to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, ensuring the voice does not cease and completing ten recitations (daśanāman).

At the end of life, they see a golden lotus flower appear before them; in the space of a single thought-moment, they attain rebirth there. These two sūtras seem contradictory, and commentators employ various methods to harmonize them."

I have been troubled by a lingering sense of unease regarding this reconciliation. Yesterday, while reciting the Buddha’s name, my mind suddenly opened up, and I realized that the original texts of the two sutras complement one another perfectly;

there is no need for forced harmonization. Specifically, the *Amitābha Sūtra* (Kuan-ching) permits rebirth in its reference to those who hear the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land only at the very moment of death.
According to the nine grades described in the original text, the first five grades all state that they achieve rebirth through these specific merits.

They dedicate their merit and pray for rebirth. The final four grades all state that at the moment of death they encounter a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), who explains the Pure Land for them and instructs them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha (*nien-fo*).
It can be understood that those of the lowest of the low grade had not heard [the Dharma] during their lives; it was only at the point of death that they first heard it.

Upon hearing it, they immediately began to recite the Buddha’s name; having finished reciting, they passed away. Through the power of repentance and the power of faith, both were resolute and decisive, with no further wavering.
By maintaining mindfulness, one attains rebirth in that land. If one hesitates for even a single moment at this critical juncture, it will be extremely difficult to achieve by mere chance.
As for why this has not been heard throughout one’s life, according to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, the Buddha told Maitreya:
"You and all the devas and humans of the ten directions have wandered through the five realms of existence since eternal kalpas until the present life, with birth and death never ceasing."
The Buddhas have encountered one another, and you have further been able to hear of Amitāyus Buddha. How joyful and excellent this is! I rejoice with you.

It is further said that there are many bodhisattvas who wish to hear this sutra but cannot obtain it. Furthermore, it is said that the Way of the Buddhas’ sutras is difficult to encounter and difficult to hear;
if one hears this sutra and, with faith and joy, accepts and upholds it, this is the most difficult of difficulties—nothing surpasses this difficulty. Based on this...

This sufficiently proves that this sutra is difficult to hear. If even bodhisattvas find it so, how much more so for those of inferior capacity and inferior birth who, in their daily lives, are possessed of various unwholesome deeds?
Thus, the "True Dharma" they slander must necessarily refer to the other twelve divisions of the Vaipulya (fangdeng) scriptures, and not to the various Pure Land sutras;
this can be known from the phrasing, which follows upon the preceding section concerning the inferior grade.
Regarding those who are reborn in the upper realms: although they have not slandered the Vaipulya sutras, they nevertheless possess various unwholesome states;

thus, we do not repeat the scriptural passages here. If one slanders the various sutras concerning the Pure Land, the root of doubt has already become deeply entrenched during their daily life; how then could it be completely uprooted at the time of death?

Even if there are virtuous friends to offer consolation and encouragement, their power will be too weak to provide salvation. As for the grave sins of the five heinous offenses, one might fortunately escape them.
The Net of the Dharma. At the moment of death, the signs of hell appear. (This also refers to the section on being born in the middle grade of the lower level; therefore, it is not repeated here.

When oppressed by suffering and seeking rescue, one must personally confess the root of one's transgressions for a virtuous friend to be able to recognize them and preach the Dharma to provide consolation.
If one has committed many grave offenses, one will soon encounter royal punishment; who then could provide such special protection as to allow one to die of illness? Furthermore, consider Ajātaśatru.
O King, you have long heard of the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land. Yet, when your rebellious deeds were not yet completed, you sought the Buddha in deep remorse;
only after the Buddha personally granted you confession (*kṣamāpana*) were you able to be freed from your transgressions.

Thus, it can be known that the "good friends" encountered by those of the three grades of the lowest class must themselves have realized the Holy Path before they can provide instruction and deliverance—unlike ordinary lecturers. Furthermore, the various sutras...

In the scriptures, there are many accounts of the merit of reciting and chanting; it can be understood from this that even those who might otherwise have been spared from execution were not comparable to those who commit the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*).

Furthermore, regarding those whom the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* does not permit to attain rebirth, this refers specifically to those who, during their daily lives, had already heard the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land.
According to the text, Amitābha attained Buddhahood ten *kalpas* prior to Śākyamuni’s own enlightenment. When [Amitābha] first resolved to attain enlightenment...
Furthermore, it was required that he pass through inconceivable billions of *kalpas* before his vow could be fulfilled and he attained Buddhahood.
Thus, it should be understood that when it is said that one slanders the True Dharma, this refers specifically to the Original Vow and not to all the sūtras spoken by Śākyamuni.
Although one may still slander it upon hearing it and thus fail to attain birth [in the Pure Land], one can still perform repentance. This was the initial position of Vasubandhu Bodhisattva.
Having slandered the Mahāyāna, he later regretted his actions and wished to cut out his own tongue. His elder brother, Asaṅga, exhorted him to transform his slander into praise;
he then performed a true repentance and subsequently composed the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* and other works, thereby accomplishing the path of a Bodhisattva. This is the proof of this principle.

If one commits the five heinous crimes intentionally and with full knowledge, one will certainly fall into hell and undergo immeasurable suffering for many kalpas. This is clearly stated in the sūtras.

The text states: "Even if one attempts to escape through external conditions, the karmic adversary cannot be avoided; yet because the seeds of one's nature have been extinguished, they cannot sprout again. Therefore, this does not admit of repentance.
Each of the two sutras clarifies a distinct meaning, precisely manifesting the power and function of the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land opened by Amitābha’s Great Vow.

This gate is supreme in its worldly truth and perfect in its efficacy. It is difficult for sentient beings to hear and faithfully accept it; thus, it shall remain as a unique teaching for the future."
The gravity of this connection is truly beyond anything inconceivable found in all other sutras.

From its initial translation during the Cao Wei period until the present, more than sixteen hundred years have passed; yet among both monastics and laypeople, those who have heard of, upheld, read, or recited the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* are rare.
That this teaching is difficult to encounter and difficult to believe has already been clearly proven. How could the Buddha...
Is this not empty talk? How could those who possess wisdom fail to reflect upon it?

The two teachings universally employ metaphors to show that emptiness and existence support one another; they are boundless and inexhaustible. Taking this as the foundation for establishing the teachings, the Middle Way is thereby revealed. The teachings arise from dependent origination.
What are its conditions? Over the course of many billions of years and among many billions of beings, the human mind has formed its attachments.

When the time arrives and the principle becomes manifest, a sage appears and establishes [the teaching] accordingly. It is the natural law; it was not intentionally contrived from the beginning, existing spontaneously with the birth of the people.

Sensual desires open wider day by day; clever ingenuity emerges day by day; changes and calamities shift day by day. Nurturing desires and providing for needs grow more and more flourishing day by day;
regulations, adjustments, and refinements also become increasingly orderly day by day. It is like constructing a house: the beams, pillars, rafters, and brackets vary in length and size.
The walls, windows, thickness, and width were all made to correspond with the ground.

Those who used axes, those who pared, those who used saws, those who used chisels, those who carved, and those who applied plaster worked in succession until the various elements were roughly complete. Upon the master builder’s direction, a grand mansion was finally accomplished.

It is not that the ordinary craftsman is clumsy, but that the master craftsman is skillful. When the time has not yet arrived, things are not yet complete; when things are not yet complete, it is because the time has not yet arrived.
Once the time arrives, they become complete; once they are complete, the time has arrived. This is the natural law, for such is the nature of dependent origination.
It was I, Confucius, who was born during the Spring and Autumn period. From the advent of written records until now, the compositions of the various sages have been gathered into a grand synthesis;

thus, I am titled the "Supreme Sage. Śākyamuni’s descent into birth occurred more than a hundred years prior; he inherited the transformative rituals and bequeathed teachings of the seven Buddhas of the past.

The Way is universally one; therefore, he is called the Dharma King. As for the sequence of their appearance—whether in the Middle Kingdom or in Western India—it is because the karmic conditions of sentient beings have ripened differently, leading to distinct manifestations of his traces.
While he established teachings according to what was appropriate, the great intent remains uniform. How is it that they are uniform?
Just as when a house has been completed, its owner, together with his retinue down to the servants and slaves, takes every step within this house upon empty ground;
every piece of furniture he places therein is upon empty ground; and in every direction and location, left and right, it is nothing but empty ground.
Arrange them in proper order from top to bottom; let it be fitting and appropriate, leaving no empty space. At the outset, do not place them upon beams or pillars, nor between walls.
When establishing one’s dwelling and securing one’s life, one likewise does not distinguish, thinking, "this is a beam or pillar," or "that is a wall."
What were the regulations? Including all the prior efforts in earthworks and timber construction, through such arduous toil this was achieved;

yet who contributed these strengths has been entirely forgotten. Only the ledgers recorded by the master craftsmen remain, detailing the allocation of various materials and the precise measurements of their expansion and contraction.

As for the dimensions of their structural frameworks, whether broad or narrow, large or small, they are clearly distinguished. Subsequent imitations adapt according to the specific site, yet do not deviate from the fundamental proportions.
From the above analogies, the general principles of the Confucian teachings can be understood through comparison; the same applies to Buddhism.
They assist one another in their functions, and the teachings are divided into five periods. Through skillful means, the nature of the mind is revealed;

because this nature of the mind, depending on time and place, is neither localized nor non-localized and is difficult to express in words, it is like the owner of a house who suddenly encounters someone asking for directions.
Regarding the house you previously built, it was constructed from thousands upon thousands of pieces of earth and wood, piled and heaped together. Do you not find it obstructive to dwell within it?
The master then replied: "The interior of the house is spacious and open; I enjoy its use with complete freedom. As for what I previously labored to create—the beams, pillars, rafters, and brackets—"

There are walls and windows, yet they form only an outer perimeter; what is there to obstruct? He asked the host again, "You say it is vast and open, with no obstructions at all, and thus you attain mastery.
Are those former earth, wood, and plaster not, then, illusory transformations? Or are they merely within the great void?"
"Can it be constructed? He replied, "No, no. My house truly exists; it is not like the 'transformed city.
In the great void of space, there is nowhere to set foot, so how could it be established? My sovereignty rests upon solid ground. He then questioned the master once more.
"The outer perimeter of this dwelling was accomplished by your strength; therefore, it is your own possession. As for the level ground upon which it stands, it does not concern your strength.
Who would allow you to occupy it? He replied, "This land was bequeathed to me by my ancestors; it is vast and boundless, its limits unknown."

Wherever a house is located, it is entirely a product of worldly craftsmanship. He further questioned the owner: "The house rests upon level ground; its upper and lower parts, as well as its four sides, are perfectly aligned and regular.
Its interior is truly empty, yet this emptiness is not the great void of space; it functions in mutual dependence with the earth. This emptiness and the earth—"

"Is there any distinction between this and the space outside the house? He replied, "There is no distinction. Again he asked, "Your mastery over both earth and space is no different from that which exists outside the house;
if there is no difference between the empty space inside and outside, then the house is established in vain, and all your previous labor was for nothing."

[The questioner] says: "I have not encountered many such matters. [The Master] replies: "No, no. Outside the house, the empty space extends as far as the eye can see; it is vast and desolate, with nothing to return to.

Because one perceives this emptiness, one becomes increasingly restless and lacks self-mastery. Yet within this very house, the interior and the exterior space support one another; having been accustomed to this for so long, one fails to realize it."
Having received your inquiry regarding the house, I am now suddenly enlightened. Thus I know that my long-standing enjoyment of ease and mastery has entirely depended upon having a house.

Although the house is but an external shell, it originally functions in inseparable mutual dependence with the open space; dwelling within it brings peace, and it is not a matter of excessive concern.
Furthermore, he asked: "By whose power is such enjoyment sustained? He replied:

"I reflect that the empty space within my house, though it has existed there from the beginning without being increased by even a single inch, is not manifested and cannot be enjoyed without the house; thus, through successive investigation, [I find its source]."

This is the power of the Great Master. Now, the records of the management and accounts noted by the Treasure-Holder are transmitted to his descendants and disseminated throughout the world, so that all may equally attain mastery.
The preceding analogies allow the general principles of the Buddha’s teaching to be understood through comparison; thus, one knows that this applies to all teachings.
It does not go beyond emptiness and existence. Existence does not exist by itself; emptiness does not exist by itself.

To see emptiness within existence, and to see existence within emptiness, they manifest each other and conceal each other, such that the Middle Way is perfectly evident. When even the Middle Way is forgotten, this constitutes the ultimate attainment. Such is the gradual progression of practice.

They still remain within the two extremes. From this, we know that when worldly people variously portray Confucius as a Buddha or scrape away the Buddha to make him a Confucian star, pitting one against the other, it all results in mere frivolous discourse (*prapañca*).
From this, we further know that only Confucius and the Buddha are inseparable and do not constitute two distinct entities.
Their union is not a single entity; both have descended through the ages and must not be neglected as one to the exclusion of the other.

From this, we know that outside of Confucius and the Buddha, there is certainly no other teaching that can be ranked alongside them as a third. For existence and emptiness are common to the human mind, and the nature of physical phenomena is likewise so.
Apart from emptiness and existence, there is no third alternative. Looking universally at all things, one should calm the mind and quiet the breath toward those with divergent views;
examine this with careful scrutiny. This concludes the miscellaneous discourse.

The proponents of the School of Principle (Lixue) say: "When the vital energy (*qi*) gathers, there is birth; when the vital energy disperses, there is death. There is no such thing as rebirth (*saṃsāra*).
Many in the world believe this and regard it as a profound principle. They do not realize that whether one is a good person or an evil person, most cannot avoid death.

It may still be acceptable to say that after a good person dies, they return to the Great Void (*tài-xū*). But after an evil person dies, do they also return to the Great Void? If they do return, would they find joy there?
When one commits evil, if it does not return, where does it abide? If you say its energy is dissipated and almost entirely exhausted, then in this state of extinction, is there any void or space?
If there is void space, it remains the great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*). If there is no void space, it remains within the single breath of vital energy (*ekaprāṇa*).
What do you mean by "extinction"? It is as you have described: it seems to return one to the Great Void. To exist eternally and not perish would be superior;
to be utterly extinguished and exhausted would be inferior. Yet, if it is the Great Void, who receives the superior state? If it is total extinction, who receives the inferior state?
Since the retribution for good and evil could not be applied at all, your arguments would be mutually contradictory; how then can you establish a teaching?

People today do not recognize their own minds; this is why they do not believe in the Buddha. Regarding these six points above, those within the gate should naturally understand them with perfect clarity.
When outsiders first hear that "thoughts are the function" and that there is a separate mind which is the "essence," they will surely be greatly startled.
We must now employ a metaphor to clarify this: the mind is like a mirror, and thoughts are like the reflections in the mirror.
The light of this [mind] reflects upon the east, the west, the beautiful, and the ugly—just as the light of a mirror reflects the east, the west, the beautiful, and the ugly.
If one were to eliminate all names and objects of form that can be spoken by the mouth or seen by the eyes, then there would be nothing from which thoughts could arise.
One can thus see that the east, the west, the beautiful, and the ugly within the movement of thought are entirely external.
The shadow of an object falls within the radiance of the mind, yet it is not the substance of the mind. Nevertheless, the substance of the mind cannot be sought after, nor can it be grasped;

it is not as easily distinguished as the substance of a mirror. For as soon as one wishes to seek it out or grasp it, that is already a thought, and one has long since fallen upon the radiance rather than upon the substance of the mind.
Question: Since it is said that apart from thought there exists a separate essence of mind, yet this essence cannot be sought out or pointed to, by what means can it be verified?
Answer: It is verified precisely by means of the thought itself. It is like a large mirror suspended within a room.

On all four sides, its boundaries are not revealed. Those outside the door do not know there is a mirror, yet when they suddenly see the reflections of their own bodies and all other objects appearing clearly before them, they immediately ascertain that a mirror exists.

Now, if one can realize the existence of the mirror's substance by means of the light reflecting images—even without seeing the mirror itself—then it is likewise possible to realize the existence of the substance of the mind without seeing it.
Regarding the illumination of objects by mindfulness, one realizes that it possesses a substantial essence.

Question: A mirror is composed either of copper or glass, and therefore it can emit light. The mind, however, has no form or substance; from where does its light originate? Answer: This question is excellent;
it allows one to recognize the nature of consciousness. Generally, when any object reaches the ultimate state of emptiness and purity, it possesses [this capacity].

Radiance. It is like fire (though it would originally have been illustrated by clouds, oceans, and mirror-light; because those are rarely perceived, I have temporarily borrowed the metaphor of fire. In reality, fire has no self-substance and bears a certain resemblance to the conscious spirit;

those with clear eyes may discern this). When evenness is ultimate and purity is ultimate, there is radiance like water. When density is ultimate and solidity is ultimate, there is radiance like the five metals or jade and stone.
The mind has no form or appearance that can be described; these six qualities—emptiness, purity, stillness, evenness, solidity, and density—are its nature.

Because this nature exists, it is not the same as inert emptiness. Therefore, one should know that this nature arises from the mind. In the text, the character for "mind" (心) is on the left and "arising" (生) is on the right;
the sound [of the characters] encompasses their meaning. Furthermore, one should know that all things have their respective analogies.
These six [elements] borrow the analogies of physical objects for inference, yet in reality they are not like those objects. As for their emptiness, nothing at all can obstruct it. Its...
It is pure; nothing can defile it. It is level; nothing can raise or lower it.
It is still; nothing can disturb or confuse it. It is firm; nothing can destroy or break it. It is dense;
nothing can penetrate or enter between its parts. Therefore, it is said that the nature is good. —From Liu Zongyuan’s “Eulogy on the Great Mirror Chan Master.”

The inscription on the stupa stele says: "In his teaching of others, he began with the ultimate good and ended with the ultimate good; without requiring weeding or tilling, he took their inherent stillness as the foundation.
This may truly be called 'knowing how to speak.'"
Now, "mind" (*xin*) functions as "recollection" (*nian*). This term combines both its phonetic and semantic aspects; the *Shuowen jiezi* states that "now" (*jin*) refers to a time of urgency.

In the world, nothing is more urgent than recollection—for example, when recollecting Amitābha Buddha. As soon as the subsequent recollection arises, the preceding recollection has already ceased. If one investigates with subtle discernment:

at the moment of recollecting the character *A*, the recollection of the character *Fo* (Buddha) has already ceased; at the moment of recollecting the character *Mi*, the character *A* has already ceased.
When one contemplates the syllable *ḍha*, the syllable *mi* has already ceased; when one contemplates the syllable *na*, the syllable *ḍha* has already ceased.

Thus, with every phrase and every syllable, they arise at that very spot and perish at that very spot. Consequently, every thought-moment (*kṣaṇa*) is the present, yet every thought-moment is the past, and every thought-moment is the future.
Since the three time periods are all ungraspable, ultimately what thing could be permanent?
Regarding cessation: if there were nothing that is eternally abiding and non-ceasing, then there would likewise be no three time periods of past, present, and future.

That the four seasons succeed one another without end constitutes the eternal abiding of heaven. That the five directions shift their positions without confusion constitutes the eternal abiding of earth.

(Heaven has no substantial entity; earth undergoes change and cessation; these are merely borrowed as metaphors. Humans are born in imitation of heaven and earth, yet their moments of thought do not cease for an instant.
If this is so, then there is nothing that exists alone, eternally abiding and indestructible. This principle is worthy of deep reflection.

During the Warring States period, the prevailing doctrines were those of Yang Zhu and Mo Di; Mencius refuted and expelled them in only one or two hundred words, yet their teachings were subsequently extinguished.
Today, only their books remain (the works of Yang Zhu being preserved as appendices in the *Liezi*), and their lineages have not been transmitted.
The Buddha-dharma entered China nearly two thousand years ago.

From the Han and Wei dynasties through to the Tang, Confucian scholars attacked it, yet they managed only a superficial description (the general outlines of the refutation of Buddhism during the Han and Wei periods can be seen briefly in Mouzi). When the Song Confucians emerged, they felt that this was still insufficient to subdue [Buddhism].
Consequently, they ventured slightly beyond its borders, engaging with its refined principles as well, yet they employed clever sophistry and loathsome vilification. This...
This tradition has been passed down until today without ceasing; it may be called the ultimate flourishing.

In the interim, it further underwent the violence of three "Wu" emperors (Emperor Wudi of the Wei, Emperor Wu of the Liu Song, and Emperor Wuzong of the Tang), who established prohibitions and destroyed it. Yet, to this day, the Buddha-dharma remains as it was throughout the land.
From the gentry scholars down to the common people, whether wise or foolish, all resolutely consider it insufficient [to be discarded].
Among those who have faith, not even one or two in a thousand can be found. Now, the doctrines of Yang Zhu and Mo Di filled the world, and their calamity was indeed fierce;

yet Mencius refuted them with such ease. Had Buddhism truly brought calamity to China, its harm over the past two thousand years would have been inexhaustible—far exceeding that of Yang and Mo by more than a hundredfold. Yet, by the sovereign’s power, the various Confucian scholars...
First, his precision in analyzing principles and the rigor with which he maintains his arguments could not move [the opponent] even by a hair’s breadth.
I do not know whether the mind, thought, and talent of those who attempted to refute him had not yet reached their full potential, or whether his Way was truly incapable of being refuted.
One of these two must necessarily be the case. If it were truly incapable of being refuted, then please do not use Mencius as a precedent.
Using such pretexts, you allow for what has not yet been fully realized; even the words of a madman are recounted by the Sage, as detailed in the following section.
I hope you will examine this with an impartial mind.
At present, the Dharma-gate has reached its extreme decline; only its coarse traces remain. I venture to offer a brief discussion based on these very traces.

In the provinces, prefectures, and counties, the number of monastics totals approximately four hundred combined. Those who rely on them for their livelihood, such as incense-makers and others, number about one hundred.
Thus, across the roughly one thousand three hundred and odd provinces, prefectures, and counties, the total comes to over sixty thousand.
Ten thousand people. These more than six hundred thousand people do not plow for their food nor spin silk for their clothing; truly, this is lamentable.

Upon closer examination, it has been exactly thus year after year from the Wei and Jin dynasties until the present. Even by the end of the Tang dynasty, the number would have exceeded several times this amount.
Suppose that throughout these one thousand eight hundred and odd years, every prefecture and county in the empire had, on average, six...
Over one hundred thousand starving people require relief for an entire year; I fear that even a sage could not remain at ease for a single day.

Recently, several provinces in both the north and south have suffered from famine, and the state has released its treasuries while officials and gentry have encouraged the distribution of grain, totaling approximately two million taels of gold.
Within less than two years, these resources have already been exhausted with such haste and urgency. Only then do we realize...
The teaching on the merit of giving to fields of fortune (*puṇyakṣetra*) is intended as a long-term strategy to break open the bag of stinginess;

it is certainly not for the sake of private self-interest. This is because the meaning of Han Yu’s “On the Way” (*Yuandao*) is expressed with strict and solemn diction, yet he invariably concludes by stating that widows, widowers, orphans, the solitary, and the disabled must have their sustenance—surely knowing the reason for this.
Among these more than six hundred thousand monastics, those who are utterly destitute and without refuge account for seven or eight parts in ten;

those who abandon themselves out of resentment account for two or three parts in ten; and those who either flee from their offenses or indulge in idleness, falling between these two categories, account for one or two parts in ten.
Those who truly understand the principles of the Buddha and act accordingly cannot be found even once in a thousand. Most merely harbor a superficial admiration for its reputation.
Among a hundred such people, perhaps one might attain it. Considering these various categories, for the most part, the rural folk are ignorant and their natures are coarse and uncultivated.
Even if we were to gather a group of such rural folk every year within our Academy’s charitable school and instruct and supervise them;
After the lapse of eighteen hundred years, those who have not fallen into ruin are few indeed.

Yet today, among them, nine out of ten can at least recognize characters, and twelve or thirteen out of ten can roughly manage brush and ink. Moreover, they all strive to conform to established boundaries and are somewhat proficient in etiquette.
Those who borrow the Dharma to peddle wickedness may perhaps number two or three in every hundred; they act openly as such.
Those who are utterly devoid of any sense of shame or restraint are but one or two in a thousand.

Yet among them, those who transcend their peers, penetrate the Great Way, possess both realization and understanding in perfect harmony, and stand preeminent as patriarchs of a generation are so numerous that one cannot count them on a single finger, as recorded in the historical annals of successive dynasties, the collected works of former sages, and the lamp histories of various lineages. Only then can one truly know the era of a single age.

The excellence of its regulations and prohibitions, its various expositions on the retribution of cause and effect regarding transgressions and blessings, and the ingenuity of its systematization and transformation truly accord with the legacy of the ancient and flourishing kings who first provided for the people's sustenance and subsequently taught them.

When Master Mingdao performed a vegetarian feast for the monks at a certain temple or observatory, he marveled that the ritual laws of the Three Dynasties were entirely contained therein; it was because he understood this history that he spoke thus.
The Indian script is similar to those of various Western nations; it consists only of phonetic sounds and lacks inherent meaning.

The Tripiṭaka—comprising the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma—is entirely a record of oral teachings. When translating, one first masters the language and replaces it with Chinese words, subsequently composing the text in Chinese characters.
Since there are differences in skill between the oral translators and the scribes, the various scriptures...

There are several versions of these texts translated at different times, both earlier and later, which differ in their detail and brevity; yet their general purport remains the same, as can be seen in the six translations of the *Vajracchedikā*.
Regarding the various mantras, it is traditionally said that there are five reasons why they are not translated (*pañca-avyavahāra*).

Some claim that they are like military passwords, permitted only for secret transmission and thus forbidden from being translated. Others claim that a single phrase may encompass multiple meanings, and therefore cannot be fully translated. Various...
All such explanations are merely conjectures. This is because the Indian language contains terms that do not exist in the Chinese language, such as names of persons, places, and objects;
when translating books from various Western nations into the present day, one can only approximate their pronunciation but cannot replace it with corresponding characters.
Furthermore, the books of various Western nations contain the names of Chinese persons and places.
It is likewise so. For instance, "Zhongyuan" (Central Plains) is referred to as "Caina. In reality, that country never previously had the name "Zhongyuan";
it is merely a phonetic transcription of those two characters. The Buddhist scriptures refer to Zhongyuan as "Zhina," which is precisely analogous to "Caina"—both are phonetic transcriptions.
When people of old could not understand the original language of a mantra, there was nothing to translate; they simply... [created] them anew.

Regarding the doctrine of the "Five Non-Translations," scholars seeking every flaw and opening have consequently slandered it as being necessarily shallow and crude, using these non-translations to conceal their own incompetence;

This refers to the vision of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the eight classes of spirits and deities.
The scope of what is heard differs from that of ordinary people; the translators did not understand this and could only preserve the original intent.

That no disciples have ever spoken these mantras since their inception is clear proof of this. The names and categories of the four fruits and the eight classes of beings do not belong to the same class as those of ordinary worldlings and are difficult to substitute with written characters;

The term "China" is a name for a person. As for the term *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta*, although only the word "citta" (mind) is translated, the single word "citta" corresponds to the Chinese "you" (to have/possess). Therefore, it can be translated.

This repetition of the second and third times, when read, makes one perceive the World-Honored One’s earnest compassion;

These are characters, comparable to Chinese poetry, admonitions, or inscriptions.

As for their written form, they resemble miscellaneous investigations and discursive treatises; medical texts on hemorrhoids that occasionally mention prescriptions or incantations used to cure disease by sprinkling water.
When these are compiled into books in China, they fall into the category of "arts and crafts" (yishu) and are likewise not regarded as weighty within the Buddhist tradition.
However, while they share the same straightforward, prosaic style, they lack all the formal structures of Chinese literary composition; thus, one cannot help but categorize them generally as follows:

Reflect calmly upon this yourself: where does the reason for this lie?
The difficulty in discerning the inner thoughts and outward conduct of the ancient sages is perhaps most evident in the case of Wu Taibo.

He renounced his sovereign and his parents, fleeing far away with his younger brother; he did not return to visit them when they were ill, nor did he hasten to their funerals. Furthermore, he cut off his hair and tattooed his body, even going so far as to go naked as an ornament.

Had it not been for these words of Confucius—if such words existed but were not seen in the *Lunyu*, appearing only in other books—I fear that even today there would be few who could affirm them rather than deny them. Right and wrong are not easily determined. The various [scholars] of the Song dynasty...
The worthy [officials] mostly searched through the Buddhist scriptures, some doing so for as long as ten years or more. At the end, they would say:

It is not necessary to read their books to see that if they truly cause the constant patterns of human relations (*yilun*) to perish, this would be a coarse manifestation of evil, evident and clearly visible.
Yet, it was only after more than ten years had passed that this was first noticed; how could such a thing be possible?
It is clear, therefore, that this did not originate from their own hearts. As for the Buddha’s regulations, he ordained that laymen and laywomen who receive the five precepts [must observe them].
One must first consult with and inform one’s parents, then one’s kinsmen, and then the sovereign; only after all have granted their permission may the precepts be expounded.
For one who desires to leave the household life, these precepts serve as the foundation. At the time of renunciation, one again formally informs the parents, kinsmen, and sovereign;
only after they have all granted their permission may one undergo tonsure and ordination to receive and uphold the śrāmaṇera precepts. After five years of training and mastery, one may advance.
The Bhikṣu precepts are practiced for seven years before one advances to the Bodhisattva precepts.

Those who may not receive the full ordination but participate in the Dharma assemblies are called Upāsakas (Pure Faith Men) and Upāsikās (Pure Faith Women). therefore, within the monastic community, seniority is reckoned by *śīla-varṣa* (years of ordination), not by actual age.

The fourfold assembly of lay followers would likewise enter the *araṇya* during both winter and summer to listen to the lectures; they would return home when their desire for study was satisfied, and return again when they wished to be fully satiated with the Dharma—all were permitted to listen.

This was the period when the Buddha was still in the world. Following his parinirvāṇa, he established a legacy: whenever receiving the precepts, there must be exactly three persons per ordination platform;

if there are more than this, the Dharma Master incurs the offense of "excessive bestowal of the Dharma. Furthermore, those who leave the household life must necessarily shave off their beards and hair—just as I [have done].
The robes and insignia of teachers and scholars must differ from those of the common multitude; furthermore, precautions have been established to ensure that the two groups do not become confused.
Viewing the matter from beginning to end, such is their skillful means of universal adaptability, yet such is their gravity and strictness. Formerly, a guest asked me:
"If Buddhism flourishes extensively, the human race will surely perish. What is to be done? I replied: "Fortunately, there are people like you."

Otherwise, at that time, the people of the various countries being converted would have been left without a single survivor due to drought; how could [the teachings] have flowed into the Eastern Land (China)?

Will you not consider that the world might once again change back into an age of raw-flesh eating and blood-drinking? Such people have lost [the Way].
He smiled and withdrew.
Some say that since ancient times, eminent monks have generally been extraordinary beyond the common crowd—awe-inspiring and not to be approached.

For this reason, when a former scholar saw the portrait of Chan Master Guizong, which was so majestic and imposing, he sighed, "With such a physical appearance as this, his innate character must surely be [extraordinary]."
"You claim that those like Cao and Mang could bring calamity as thieves upon the world. I laughed and said: 'You are mistaken.
These are the words of former scholars praising the Buddha; you take them to be an insult? Now, both Cao and Mang were esteemed for their literary talent in their own time;

"One can thus know that the disposition of Cao Cao and Wang Mang was also of the 'returning to the source' (guīzōng) type.

Whether the entry of Buddhism into China brought harm or benefit? The questioner laughed, apologized, and departed.

Regarding the study of the nature of the mind, nothing is more profound and subtle than the Buddhist scriptures. Whether recording full texts or summarizing the essential principles, the myriad words of the Song Confucians are all rooted in this.
Among their most prominent major tenets are, for instance, the pairing of phenomena and principle (the two phrases from Yangzi—“In explaining phenomena, none is as detailed as the *Shujing*;
in discerning principle, none is as refined as the *Chunqiu*”—are also distinct statements of this), and the pairing of non-action with good and evil.

The essence of the mind requires forgetting both the internal and the external. The mind possesses its entirety and its great function, such that substance and function share a single source, and the manifest and the subtle are without interval.

(These are what Chengzi [Cheng Hao] meant by "that which must be spoken of when there is no other choice. All these teachings were first initiated within the commentaries and recorded sayings of the various Chan masters of the Tang dynasty.

This was because the time had arrived and the principle was revealed; those who entered [the Way] were transformed together with it, unaware of it themselves, and would surely have called it the "hidden" (yin).

To employ [these teachings] yet reject them with overt hostility is likewise an error. Those who disparage them do so because their preconceived notions regarding the Ultimate Non-being (Wuji), the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji), Yin and Yang, and the Five Elements are so firmly rooted that they cannot be uprooted;
they fail to realize that when the Six Classics, the *Analects*, and the *Mencius* speak of the nature and mind (*xingxin*), they do not originally intend such things.

[An opponent may object: "The ultimate truth becomes increasingly refined as it is further elucidated. The original *Tàijí tú* (Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate) is incorrect. The response states: "This principle is easy to understand. The first volume consists of a collection of passages from the Six Classics and the *Analects* and *Mencius*, as well as the writings on mind and nature by the various masters and schools prior to the Western Han.
The second volume consists of the writings on mind and nature by the various masters and schools from the Eastern Han onwards until the beginning of the Sui dynasty.
The third volume consists of the writings on mind and nature by the Confucian scholars of the Tang dynasty and the Five Masters who preceded the Song.

The fifth section of the Song dynasty and those down to the great masters of our own dynasty who discussed mind and nature, along with their fundamental tenets for study, constitute the Fourth Volume.

I have compiled and categorized the various accounts concerning Buddhism, including those found in historical records, imperial edicts, official memorials, and private writings.

Regarding its origins and transmission: it simply states that this is the learning of Zhouzi (Zhou Dunyi), yet it is unknown from whom his teacher-disciple lineage derived, which remains unexplained.

This is because, since the two schools of Confucianism and Buddhism have been in incessant contention, their followers often cite renowned public figures and force them into their own sectarian lineages to bolster their own positions;

This is what is meant by "entering [the other tradition] and being transformed together," such that one is not even aware of it oneself.

As for principle (*li*), it is naturally essential that one’s words not be prolix. To insist that the original source begins with *Qian* and is able to benefit the world with its sublime benefits, yet remains silent regarding what it benefits, is likewise a forced argument.

This is the essential point. It is a fallacy to speak in terms of "leakage. Now, as for the two traditions of Confucianism and Buddhism: if one separates them, they certainly do not become two; yet if one combines them, they are likewise not truly one.

This is indeed a statement made by one who knows. If one were to force connections and fabricate associations based on mere words and texts, even if one could achieve a close fit, it would still be merely borrowing the prestige of another.

This is useless and harmful. Hanshan’s commentary on the *Inner Chapters* of the *Zhuangzi*, and Ouyi’s exegesis of the *Book of Changes* and the Four Books, demonstrate great hardship in their application of effort;
yet they were unaware that Confucian scholars had long ago read the eighty fascicles of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
It would be better to read the admonition of a single hexagram line from the *Gèn* (艮) rather than this. This trend has flowed down to the present day;

people constantly claim that the Three Teachings share a common source, establishing this as a heterodox doctrine that deludes the world and deceives the people, thereby sowing the seeds of disorder. When one searches for the root of this malady, it ultimately stems from a single thought:
a haste to seek credence. Driven by this, affairs have come to such a pass; therefore, I cannot help but offer a severe critique in the hope that [this will be understood].
Later worthies should take this as a perpetual, clarifying warning.
The designation of the "Three Teachings" was likely first coined by the Northern Wei Daoist Kou Qianzhi; thus, even Wenzhongzi used these two characters.
Since what is not known cannot constitute a teaching, the Laozi, who is their progenitor, is merely one among the Nine Schools.
The "Bibliography" (Yiwenzhi) of the *Hanshu* provides clear evidence for this. Throughout his life, the only work he authored was the *Daodejing* in five thousand words.

This not only stands in total contrast—like cattle and oxen separated by a vast distance—to the empty and hyperbolic doctrines of later Daoist practitioners, but it also differs significantly from the teachings of Zhuangzi and Liezi.
As for the *Changqingjing* currently practiced by the secular world, it was composed by a student of Chan Buddhism during the Tang dynasty.
These are false attributions. Their literary style, phrasing, and characters do not resemble the language of the Spring and Autumn period at all; they are extremely easy to distinguish.
As for scriptures such as the *Lingbao* texts, these were all forged successively by figures such as Kou Qianzhi, Bao Jing, and Lin Lingsu.

They entirely plagiarized the more superficial elements of Buddhist scriptures, even going so far as to copy their phrasing and cadence verbatim. Former sages have long since thoroughly exposed them, and their origins and lineages are well known.
The various accounts are inconsistent. Mr. Fang Weidien’s preface to the *Baozhu zi* provides the most detailed examination and discussion (appended below).

What is particularly laughable is that among the various mantras of the Buddhist tradition, many characters are written with the radical for "mouth" (口). This is because the Chinese script lacks those specific characters;
they can only be replaced by combining several characters to approximate the sound. Those characters bearing the "mouth" radical must be pronounced with a retroflex (retracted tongue) articulation.
This is merely a mark used to indicate pronunciation, similar to the circles added to characters in Confucian texts; it is not that the character itself possesses a circle.
Furthermore, these "incantation characters" (zhòuzì) were forged by Daoists and frequently feature the radical for "mouth. One must ask: were Laozi and the so-called Yuan Shitian foreigners?
The lineage of Zhang Tianshi was originally not part of the Daoist tradition, but rather that of the shamans and ritualists of the Zhou dynasty.
This is the bequeathed dharma [of the immortals]. It was capable of communicating with ghosts and spirits, but it was lost during the transition between the Qin and Han dynasties.

Later, it was acquired by the Yellow Turban rebels, the brothers Zhang Jue and his kin. Zhang Daoling was a direct descendant of Zhang Jue; the method for communicating with ghosts and spirits he employed was still the ancient rite.
Subsequent generations failed to preserve and observe it faithfully. Seeing that the fraudulent sects of secular Daoists were flourishing, they further...
To compare them: the four characters [竺-二+齕] [竺-二+(齒*其)] [竺-二+齪] [竺-二+(齒*定)] were created by a heterodox practitioner during the Jiajing era of the Ming dynasty.
Yet today, the Temple of the Heavenly Master (Tianshi Fu) also employs them as part of its "Correct Dharma. This is truly enough to make one burst with laughter.

Fang Wei Dian’s preface to the *Baopuzi* states that the fundamental tenets of the Daoist school consist simply of purity, serenity, and profound emptiness. Its corruptions have sometimes flowed into the realm of political stratagems and sometimes into licentious extravagance;

it contains no such things as elixirs of gold and cinnabar, immortal medicines, the transformation of base metals into gold and silver, nor practices of breath cultivation, physical gymnastics, or ritual prohibitions.
This is the art of incantations, talismans, and registers (*zhufu-lu*). The fangshi (masters of esoterica) of the Qin and Han dynasties never associated these with Laozi;

even their reliance upon the Yellow Emperor (*Huangdi*) was not a teaching of the Daoist school. The "Bibliographic Treatise" (*Yiwenzhi*) of the *Book of Han* (*Hanshu*) assigns the various chapters concerning the Yellow Emperor to the Daoist category.
This classification of the immortals (*shenxian*) is fundamentally based on the *Qielüe* (Seven Summaries), which in turn was derived from the *Bielu* (Separate Records). Liu Ziyong...
Those who diligently recited and studied the *Hongbao* (Great Treasures) and firmly believed in the immortals were appointed to collate and verify the Secretaries’ Archives;

furthermore, they categorized the arts and techniques (*fangji*) separately from the Miscellaneous Writings (*zizi*), so as not to confuse them. Toward the end of the Eastern Han, Emperor Huan was fond of immortals and offered sacrifices to Laozi;

"There are things people desire more than life itself, and things they loathe more than death itself; everyone possesses these, and it is only the worthy who are able not to lose them.

It is utterly so. Yet, though one may desire it to the extreme, life can never be obtained by mere whim; though one may loathe it to the extreme, death can never be avoided by mere whim.

"By practicing all wholesome dharmas without [the notions of] self, person, sentient being, or life-span, one attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Its third proof is from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
The language of worldly affairs and the means of livelihood for sustaining life are all non-contradictory with the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). There are four such proofs;

This is spoken solely from the perspective of the eternally abiding *dharmakāya*, which has never actually entered [the world] in the first place—what, then, could be said of it?

As for the equality of the Buddha-dharma, it means that all things are fundamentally equal from the beginning. Now, by causing each to return to its original position, it is called the equality of the Buddha-dharma.

It is precisely within this state of non-selection and non-arrangement that one must bring one’s practice into a single seamless whole. What is it that one intimately realizes?

When things come, respond in accordance with them; this is how they were roughly understood. Lately, a certain kind of demonic influence has misinterpreted these two phrases, and has further misinterpreted the two phrases from the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:

The milk of the Dharma. Having but meager roots of faith, I could not bear to sit idly by as others were swept away, betraying the shared endowment of all sentient beings.

Six Verses on Opening the Mind through the Recitation of the Buddha’s Name by Master Buyu Recite the Buddha’s name to seek rebirth in the Pure Land.
Each thought encompasses the Three Baskets of the Canon. One must strictly avoid a wandering mind. Do not harbor self-doubt or cling to appearances.
Do not look for words in the fundamental texts; focus your mindfulness exclusively and single-mindedly on the Buddha, seeking rebirth through constant recollection.
In every thought-moment, the merit and wisdom will accumulate. One must strictly avoid an inferior mind that harbors self-doubt, thinking one will not succeed.
The original text does not state that the mind’s activity is itself the mind.

One should practice mindfulness of the Buddha seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, with every thought in accord with the Buddha’s vow. One must strictly avoid a desire for haste, which leads to self-doubt regarding the efficacy of the practice.
Do not look for words in minor texts; at the moment of death, the Buddha will appear in person.

Recite the Buddha’s name seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, so that every thought enters the Buddha’s wisdom. Most strictly avoid a mind of clever discernment; if you harbor self-doubt, you remain mired in delusion.
If you do not see the Buddhas of the six directions, they will protect you so that you never fall back.
By recollecting the Buddha and seeking rebirth, your transgressions are extinguished with every thought-moment. You must absolutely avoid a heart of fear and self-doubt that you lack efficacy.
Do not look for the judgment of the Original Teacher; those of inferior capacity are often full of malice and rebellion.

By reciting the Buddha's name to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, one realizes purity and fulfillment in every thought-moment. One must strictly avoid a calculating mind that doubts the shallowness of one’s own practice and understanding.

The Eulogy for the Immortal Pavilion (with preface recorded separately):

The Layman Wuxiang plays at ease within the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*). Having cast off the hindrances of the mundane world like a cicada shedding its shell, he possesses manifold roots of goodness and the causal conditions of merit and virtue.
He turns the wheel of his original vows. There is a great jeweled pavilion, adorned with pure bliss, complete with the eight treasuries.

Together with those of like kind, he examines and organizes the principles within it, extracting the essentials and probing the profound origins. Through this Dharma-joy, he contemplates the essence of all teachings; they are comparable to that jeweled pavilion.

The essence is fundamentally unborn. Earth, wood, vermilion, and green—the constant speaking and listening—this pavilion is likewise fundamentally illusory. Ascending and descending amidst its radiant splendor is nothing but the contemplation of the mind.
What is this contemplation of the mind? It is the convergence of the twenty-three categories at the ultimate limit of *Susumā*; it is the counting of one’s own household treasures.
